turns.content: So welcome back. How are things?

Hi. Thanks. I mean, I'm okay, I guess. Things have been a bit up and down since I last talked to someone about this. The whole video game expo thing still feels pretty fresh in my mind, if I'm being honest.
Yeah. So how do you feel about going back there again now?

Honestly? The thought makes me feel a bit sick. I keep replaying that final match in my head, thinking about all the mistakes I made. I just know if I went back, I'd probably mess up again and let everyone down.
What if we explored that together? What would need to happen for you to say, "I can't go back"?

I guess... if I knew for sure that I'd be the reason my team lost again. Like, if I practiced every day for a month and still made the same dumb errors under pressure. That would just prove that I'm not cut out for competing, you know?
And so going back wouldn't matter because you're just going to make the same mistakes anyway.

Exactly. It feels like no matter how much I prepare, when the pressure's on, I just freeze up and make bad calls. I don't even want to try anymore because I already know how it'll end — with me feeling like I dragged everyone down again.
Well, maybe we could look at whether you really think that would actually be the case.

I mean, I know it sounds pretty black-and-white when you say it like that. But that's just how it feels — like it's already decided before I even start. I can't shake the thought that I'm just not good enough to compete at that level.
Can we explore that together? Can you give me an example of a situation where you've felt like you weren't good enough to compete at some other high-pressure event?

Hmm... well, there was this one time in college when I had to present a group project. I was so nervous I stumbled over my words, and I felt like everyone in the room was judging me. After that, I just assumed I was terrible at public speaking and avoided it whenever I could.
Okay, so you did stumble over your words and feel judged by the audience. Wasn't that uncomfortable?

Yeah, it was awful. I could feel my face burning red, and my hands were shaking so bad I could barely hold my notes. I remember thinking, "Everyone here thinks I'm an idiot." And I just wanted the floor to swallow me up.
Okay. So you did feel really anxious and self-conscious. Were you right though, about everyone judging you?

I mean... I don't really know what they were all thinking. Nobody said anything mean to me afterwards, if that's what you're asking. But I just assumed they were being polite, you know? Like they felt sorry for me or something.
So you assume that people were judging you negatively based on how you felt during the presentation.

Yeah, I guess so. It's like my brain just jumps straight to the worst conclusion, and I don't even stop to check if it's true. With the video game thing, it's the same — I just assume everyone on my team thinks I'm the weak link now.
So if we look at both examples, you concluded that you didn't belong in those situations. Is that fair?

I suppose so. I just can't help but feel like I'm the common denominator, you know? Like if I'm the one messing up, it must be something about me that's broken. But I'm starting to see how I might be jumping to conclusions without really knowing for sure.
And so it doesn't necessarily mean that you aren't good enough to compete. Maybe there's more nuance to that than you realize.

I never really thought about it that way before. I've just been so stuck on the idea that I'm the problem that I haven't considered there might be other factors at play. Maybe I'm being too hard on myself.
Right. So you're wondering whether you might be giving yourself a harder time than you deserve.

That actually feels... kinda liberating to think about. Like maybe I don't have to carry all that blame around. But I still don't know how to stop my brain from going there automatically when things go wrong.
We could practice that together. You could notice when you're having those thoughts and ask yourself, "Is this actually true?"

That sounds like it could help. I mean, it's not like I want to keep feeling this way — it's exhausting. I'd be willing to try giving myself a little more benefit of the doubt next time I mess up, even if it feels weird at first.
Sounds good. So we could work on noticing those automatic thoughts and checking them against reality. Are you ready to take that step?
Yeah, I think I am. It's scary to change how I think about myself, but what I'm doing now isn't working anyway. I'm willing to give it a shot and see where it takes me.
Alright. Well, how does that sound? Would you be willing to try that out next week?

Yeah, I think I can do that. I'll try to catch myself when I start blaming everything on myself and just pause for a second. It sounds simple, but I know it'll be harder than it sounds. I'll give it my best shot though.

All right. We'll see how it goes. Just a quick summary of our discussion then. First, I noticed you mentioned you were anxious about going back to the competition. Then I asked you to share any experiences where you felt like you weren't good enough to compete. You gave me two examples, which led us to conclude that you may be making assumptions about others' reactions to you. And finally, we agreed to do some exercises together to challenge negative self-talk.
That sounds about right. It's helpful to hear it all laid out like that. I think I have a clearer picture now of what I need to work on. Thanks for helping me see things from a different angle.
I'm glad I could help. Good luck.
So how was yesterday?
Honestly, not great. I've been thinking a lot about the tournament, and it's really bringing me down. Every time I picture us playing, I just see us losing again.
Okay. So what do you think will happen when we play in the tournament?
I think we're going to lose. Probably badly. I mean, we already lost one game, so why would the next one be any different? Our team just doesn't have what it takes this year.
But there's more to the story than that. What else is going on here?

Well, I guess it's not just about that one loss. It's like, now I can't stop thinking about all the mistakes we made that game, and I just assume we'll make them again. Every time I think about practice, I feel like there's no point trying so hard if we're just going to fail anyway.
And what happens when you feel like there's no point trying hard? How does that affect you?

It makes me feel drained, honestly. I don't put in the same effort during practice, and I'm not as excited to play. I love basketball, but now it feels like a chore, like I'm just going through the motions until we lose again.
So, what did you learn from that first game? What were some things you did well that helped the team win the other games?

I mean, we did have some good plays... our defense was solid for most of the game, and a few of us were really on point with passing. But it's hard to hold onto that when all I can remember is that missed shot in the last quarter that sealed the loss.
Do you think those good defensive efforts and good passes will continue to come up in the future?
Maybe they will... I guess we've done it before, so it's possible. But it's like my brain just skips over that part and jumps straight to the mistakes. I don't know how to stop that from happening.
Sometimes, when I feel overwhelmed by something negative, I find myself having trouble remembering positive aspects. Have you ever tried counting backwards from ten by twos?
Counting backwards? I haven't tried that. It sounds kind of random, but I guess it could help me focus on something else instead of spiraling. What would that do, exactly?
Yeah, so imagine you're counting backwards from ten by twos, starting with ten. So ten, eight, six, four, two. You could use that to distract yourself when you're feeling anxious.

Okay, I think I get it. So it's like a way to hit pause on the negative thoughts and just focus on something simple. I'll give that a shot next time I'm at practice and start feeling that hopelessness creep in. Thanks.
I'm glad that worked out. We can talk more about that later, maybe even try it together right now?
Sure, we can try it. I'm a bit skeptical, but I'm willing to give it a go. So I just start at ten and count down by twos, out loud?
Right, yeah, say it out loud. And then after you finish, tell me how it felt.
Alright. Ten... eight... six... four... two. Okay, that was... actually kind of calming. It forced my mind to slow down for a second. I didn't think about the tournament at all during that.
Okay, I'm glad that worked. Can we write that down so you can refer back to it whenever you need it?
Yeah, that's a good idea. I'll jot it down in my phone or something. It's nice to have something simple I can do when my thoughts start to race like that.
That's perfect. And let me also know how it goes tomorrow. Does that sound okay?
Yeah, I can do that. I'll let you know if it helps me get through practice or if my brain just goes right back to the negativity. Thanks for the suggestion.
You're welcome. Well, thanks for coming in today. That's always a pleasure. Let's meet up tomorrow at the same time and talk more about the tournament. See you tomorrow.
So glad we can talk again. How have things been since we last spoke?

Honestly, not much has changed. I went on a hike last weekend with some friends and that familiar voice started up again, telling me I'm holding everyone back. It just ruined the whole experience for me.
Okay, so there was this hiking trip where you had some good experiences, but then something happened after the fact. What did it sound like when that voice came into your head?

It's like this running commentary in my head. "You're too slow, you're breathing too hard, everyone else is having a better time because of you." It just gets louder and louder until I can't focus on anything else but my own inadequacy.
Yeah, sounds like it really took away from the fun and made you feel pretty down. You were able to do anything about it once it got going though?

I tried to just push through it and tell myself to stop being so hard on myself. But it never really works. The thoughts just keep circling, and eventually I just go quiet and stop talking to the others. That's usually when someone asks if I'm okay.

Mm-hmm. So you ended up withdrawing from the group? And then they asked you how you were doing. Yeah, I think I can understand why those thoughts can be so hard to shake off. They really are pretty powerful.

Yeah, exactly. And the worst part is, I know they mean well when they ask, but I just feel like a burden. I can't even enjoy the beautiful views because I'm so caught up in my own head. It feels like my entire identity as a hiker is a fraud.
So it seems like when you're having trouble concentrating and people are around you, you start feeling like maybe you aren't as capable as you want to believe. Does that make sense?

Yes, that's it precisely. It's like I have this image in my head of what a "real" hiker is — strong, effortless, always leading the way — and I just don't match up. So instead of just being me on the trail, I'm constantly comparing myself to that impossible standard.
That's a very understandable reaction. Okay, so let me just quickly summarize what I hear you saying here. On one hand, you know that you actually enjoyed the experience of hiking with your friends.
Right, I did enjoy parts of it. The fresh air, the views, the company... until that voice takes over. Then all I can focus on is what I'm doing wrong. It's like the good parts get completely erased.
And on the other side, you've identified an idealized picture of what you'd consider a perfect hiker, which you compare yourself to. Is that accurate?

That's exactly it. It's this perfect hiker in my head who never gets tired, never needs a break, and is always smiling. And every time I can't match that, I feel like I've failed, even if I'm doing just fine by any normal standard.
Okay, so you've kind of established that there are certain beliefs that you have that lead to this behavior of disengaging socially.
Yeah, I suppose so. I never really thought of it as a pattern like that, but it does seem to go from that belief straight to me shutting down. What do I even do about that? It feels so automatic.

Well, it doesn't have to be automatic, if we work together on it. Let's try taking this to the next level and seeing if we can change some of these beliefs. Like, let's take that idea of the perfect hiker. Is that really a realistic goal? Can anyone really reach that standard?

I guess not. When you say it like that, it sounds kind of ridiculous. Nobody's perfect, and I know my friends aren't judging me the way I judge myself. But it's so hard to remember that in the moment. It feels so real.
Yeah, it's easy to think that way in the moment, but it's probably worth looking at that idea more closely. Are you sure that this isn't a little bit exaggerated?

I think you're right. I mean, when I really look at it, I've completed every hike I've ever started, even that tough one a few years ago. I didn't quit. So maybe I'm not as bad as I tell myself I am. It's just that voice makes me forget all that.

Exactly. So it seems like this internal narrative is distorting reality a bit. Maybe we could try changing it a bit by focusing on some more helpful ways of thinking about yourself. So if you were to come up with a list of qualities that are important to you when it comes to hiking, what might they be?

Well, I'd say enjoying nature is important to me. And being dependable, showing up for my friends, and not giving up even when it gets tough. Those are things I actually do, now that I think about it. I just never give myself credit for them.

That's really interesting. Because I wouldn't necessarily expect you to have all those qualities built in, especially enjoyment. But yeah, I'm not surprised that you listed those three. There's also endurance and strength, which are certainly traits that I wouldn't expect you to possess either.

I get what you're saying. I do have endurance if I've finished every hike. And I'm stronger than I give myself credit for. Maybe I need to start looking at the evidence instead of just believing that critical voice. It's just hard to remember to do that when I'm on the trail.

Right, because that voice is definitely loud and distracting. But it's not true. We can try to remind ourselves of our strengths when that happens. What do you think would happen if we worked on that?

I think it could help a lot, honestly. Maybe if I had a few things I could tell myself when that voice starts up, like a comeback or something. It might make hiking feel like mine again, instead of something I have to prove myself at. I'd like to try that.
I think that's a great idea. And it'll take practice, obviously, but I'm happy to help you brainstorm some ideas if you want.

Yeah, I'd like that. Maybe something simple like "I belong here" or "I've done this before, I can do it again." Just something to cut through the noise. I think if I can hold onto that, it might make a real difference.

That's a really nice phrase, and I like that you chose something personal and relevant. And the repetition will definitely help with the volume of that voice. Yeah, I'm happy to help you brainstorm more ideas if you want.

Thanks. I think just having that anchor, that simple phrase, feels like a good first step. I'm actually feeling a little more hopeful about my next hike. Maybe I can actually enjoy the view this time instead of just worrying.
So you're ready to try this out, and hopefully you'll find that it helps you stay engaged a bit longer. Sounds like you're ready to go home and do some prep work on your own.

Yeah, I think I am. I'll write that phrase down and maybe come up with a couple more. And I'll try to notice when I start comparing myself to that perfect hiker and gently remind myself that I'm doing okay. Thanks for helping me see this differently.
Well, thanks for sharing your thoughts with me. I hope you have a successful hike tomorrow, and I hope that your voice won't get too loud. I'm looking forward to hearing from you next week.
Hi there, I'm glad you could make it today. How have you been since we last spoke?
Hi, thanks. I've been okay, I guess. Just the usual ups and downs, but I've been thinking a lot about the stuff we talked about. I still find myself getting really down on things, you know?
Yeah, I hear you. So, do you want to talk more about how you're feeling lately, or should we look at what you were working on last time?

I think I'd like to talk about how I'm feeling. It's been a rough week with this. I tried to listen to a new album from an artist I usually love, but one song didn't hit right, and I just felt like the whole thing was a waste of time. It's like I can't help it.
So it sounds like when something doesn't go quite right, you feel pretty frustrated. What else happened this week that made you feel frustrated?

I bought this new skincare product that everyone was raving about, and after one use, my skin didn't look like perfect glass or whatever. So I just threw it in the drawer and now I'm convinced it's a total dud. Even the stuff that's supposed to make me happy just ends up feeling disappointing.

Well, yeah, I don't know about that, but let's keep going. You mentioned it's been frustrating because things aren't turning out the way you wanted them to. Can you give me some examples of other things that haven't worked out the way you expected?

Even little things, like ordering food. If I get a meal and one part of it isn't as good as I thought it'd be, I'll just feel like the whole meal was bad. Or if I'm hanging out with a friend and they seem a bit off for a few minutes, I start thinking the whole friendship is ruined. It's like my brain just latches onto one tiny flaw and blows it up.
It sounds like you're having a hard time looking at the bigger picture. And it seems like those moments where you notice that little imperfection, you blow it out of proportion.

Yeah, that's exactly it. I don't mean to, but it just happens automatically. Like, I'll be having a decent day, and then one small thing goes wrong, and I feel like the entire day was terrible. I can't seem to just let it be a small thing.

Okay. Well, so I wonder if that kind of thinking might be contributing to your low mood. So it sounds like you may have had some fun events, like watching movies, or playing games with friends, or maybe eating a delicious dinner. But instead of dwelling on those positive moments, your mind keeps focusing on the negative aspects.

Yeah, I guess you're right. I never really thought of it that way. I mean, I did have a good conversation with my friend the other day, but all I can remember now is that I felt awkward for a second when I couldn't think of something to say. It's like the good stuff just gets erased.
Yeah, it's certainly possible that focusing on the negatives makes it harder to enjoy the positives. What do you think might happen if you shifted your attention to the good parts?

I don't know, it feels kind of fake, like I'm just ignoring the bad stuff. But maybe if I tried, I'd feel less miserable about everything. I just don't know how to make myself stop noticing the flaws first.
Sometimes it takes practice to shift our attention. And I suspect we'll need to work together to figure out how best to do that.

Yeah, I guess that makes sense. I've been trying to force myself to think positive, but it never sticks. Maybe if we break it down, it'll actually work this time. I'm willing to try, 'cause I don't want to keep feeling this way.

Okay. So, let's start by exploring some of those examples you gave us earlier. Like when you ordered food and one part wasn't great, or when you were talking to a friend and noticed a moment of awkwardness. Let's start with the food. When you ordered the food, what was your initial expectation?

I guess I expected it to be perfect, like every bite would be amazing. I'd seen good reviews online and built it up in my head. So when the fries were a little soggy, it just wrecked the whole experience for me. I didn't even enjoy the burger, which was actually pretty good.
So here, the fact that one element of the meal didn't meet expectations caused you to miss out on enjoying another part of the meal.

Yeah, exactly. I didn't even give the burger a fair chance because I was so stuck on the fries. It's like my whole meal was ruined by that one thing, and I barely remember how the burger tasted. That's so dumb when I say it out loud.
Yeah, I agree. Yeah, so it does sound like you're blaming one thing for ruining the rest. Does that make sense?

Yeah, it does make sense when you put it like that. I never really thought about how I was just ignoring the good parts because of one bad part. So I guess I'm kind of doing that in a lot of areas of my life, huh?
That sounds about right. So let's take a step back and consider whether the quality of the fries or the awkward pause during that conversation actually matters. What do you think?

I mean, in the grand scheme of things, no, they don't matter at all. A few soggy fries or a weird silence isn't going to change my life. But in the moment, it feels huge, like it's all that matters. I guess I need to figure out how to remind myself that it's not that big of a deal.

Right, so it doesn't matter in the long run, but it's tough to ignore when it's happening. So what do you think would help? How do you think we could convince yourself that those moments aren't worth worrying about?

Maybe I could try writing down the good parts of something right after it happens, before my brain can pick at the bad stuff. Like, for the meal, I could've noted that the burger was great before I got hung up on the fries. Or for hanging out with my friend, I could think about the whole conversation instead of that one awkward pause. It might feel weird at first, but it's worth a shot.
So you're suggesting that jotting down the good bits of your experiences while they're fresh in your memory could help distract you from the negatives.

Yeah, something like that. It's like giving the good stuff a fighting chance, you know? Instead of letting my brain automatically trash everything, I'd have a list of proof that it wasn't all bad. I'm willing to try it for a week or so and see if it makes any difference.
Okay, sounds like a good plan. So what I'm hearing is that you're interested in seeing if keeping track of the good parts helps improve your overall outlook on things.

Yeah, I'm actually a little curious to see what happens. I mean, I've been stuck in this negative loop for a while now, so maybe just forcing myself to notice the positives will shake things up. I'll give it a try and let you know how it goes next time.

Alright, well, thank you for coming in today. Thanks for sharing all of these details with me. It's helped me understand what you're experiencing better. I'm excited to hear how it goes. See you next time!

Hi there, how are you getting on? I'm really looking forward to meeting up with you today. So, we've got about twenty minutes together, and I'd like to try to find something useful that we can work on.
Hi, thanks for having me. I'm doing okay, I guess. A bit nervous, to be honest—I've never done anything like this before. But I'm hoping it might help clear my head a bit.

That sounds great. And yeah, if you're feeling nervous, that's totally normal. It means you want to do well here. So, what do you think would be good to talk about today? What do you need to focus on?

Well, I guess it's mostly about work. I'm a freelance accountant, and lately I've been feeling like it's just not good enough, you know? Like when I talk to friends who have these stable, impressive jobs, I just feel kind of small in comparison.

Okay, so I'm going to write down 'feeling small'—that's a good summary of where you're coming from. Okay. Now, let's look more closely at that. Where do you come from in terms of that feeling? When does that start happening? Can you give me a couple examples?

I guess it really hit me about a year ago. I was at a party with some college friends, and they were all talking about their promotions and big salaries, and I was just sitting there thinking, "I'm doing taxes for small businesses from my spare bedroom." It felt like everyone else was moving forward and I was stuck.
Okay, so a year ago at a party with friends, you started to feel smaller because you had a different job than everybody else. That makes sense. What did you think then? How did that make you feel?

I felt this sinking feeling, like I'd made the wrong choices in life. I started thinking, "Maybe I'm just not ambitious enough," or "Maybe I'm too scared to go after a real career." It made me feel kind of pathetic, honestly. I ended up leaving the party early and just went home.
Okay. So that sinking feeling—that's interesting. You decided to leave the party early, and that's the behaviour, right?
Yeah, I guess so. I just didn't want to be there anymore, seeing everyone else happy with their lives. It felt like I didn't belong in that conversation.
So, you felt smaller, you thought you weren't ambitious enough, and you left the party. Is that fair?

Yeah, that's pretty much exactly it. And it's not just that one party either—it happens a lot. Even just scrolling through social media and seeing where people from college ended up, I get that same feeling all over again.
So, social media, too, triggers those feelings. Yeah. What's going on in your mind when you scroll through social media?

I start comparing, automatically. I see someone got a corner office or a fancy job title, and I think, "They made it, and I didn't." Then I start going through all the things I haven't achieved yet—steady income, benefits, respect from people. It's like my mind just zeros in on what I'm missing.
And that's where the negative thinking comes in, isn't it? It's focusing on the stuff you're missing instead of noticing everything else.

I guess so. I mean, I do have clients who appreciate my work, and I have a flexible schedule. But when I'm in that mindset, none of that seems to matter. It's like the good stuff just gets pushed aside.

Exactly. It feels like you're ignoring the positives because you're focused on the negatives. So, what would happen if you stopped being so critical of yourself and focused more on what you're actually achieving?

That's a tough question. I suppose I'd feel a bit more at peace, maybe even proud of what I've built on my own. But it's hard to break that habit, you know? I've been doing it for so long that it feels automatic now.
Yeah, that's true. The brain doesn't like change, which is why it's important to challenge those unhelpful thoughts. So, what would you say is the best way to tackle that problem?

Maybe I could try writing down one good thing about my work each day, something I actually did well. That way, I can't just ignore it completely. It might help me see things more balanced, instead of always focusing on what's missing.
That's a brilliant idea. So, you're thinking about keeping a list of achievements each day. Sounds like a good starting point. So, what would you say is the first step?

I think the first step is just to commit to it, even if it feels a bit silly at first. Maybe start tonight—write down one thing I did today that went well. Even if it's small, like finishing a report early or helping a client solve a problem. Just get into the habit.
Okay, so you'll start by writing down one positive thing about your work tonight. Great. Any other steps we should consider?

Maybe I could also try talking to my friend about this. I've been holding back because I feel ashamed, but keeping it all inside doesn't seem to be helping either. Just saying it out loud to someone might take some of the weight off.
Talking to a friend. That's another really good idea. Talking to a friend takes some of the pressure away and lets you vent.
Yeah, exactly. I think I've been isolating myself with these thoughts, and that just makes them bigger. If I can share it with someone who knows me, maybe they'll help me see it differently too.

Yeah, so sharing with a friend is definitely something that could help. So, to sum up, we've talked about writing down one good thing about your work each day and speaking to a friend about how you're feeling.
That sounds right. It feels manageable, like I could actually try those things without feeling overwhelmed. Thanks for helping me break it down.
Absolutely, and I'm really glad we could figure that out together.
Me too. I wasn't sure what to expect coming in, but I feel a bit lighter already. I'll give those steps a try this week and see how it goes.
Great. So, what you're going to do tonight is write down one thing you enjoyed about your work, and tomorrow morning, you'll speak to your friend about how you're feeling. Perfect. See you next time!
Hi there, how are you? How have you been? And if we can think about something I might want to work on together, what did you have in mind?

Hi, I'm okay I guess. Just been feeling a bit stuck lately. Honestly, I think I want to work through this fear I have about starting a new online business. After my last one failed, I just can't shake the feeling that I'm going to fail again no matter what I do.
So when you say you're stuck, what does that look like for you? What are you doing right now?

Well, I'm still working my regular marketing job, so that's fine—I can do that without panicking. But whenever I think about launching another online business, I just freeze up. I'll start brainstorming ideas, then I'll remember how much time and money I lost last time, and I'll just stop. I end up doing nothing about it for weeks.

So what's going on here? You've got some thoughts about failing and losing time and money. Those thoughts are making you feel anxious and worried, and then you end up avoiding the situation by not taking any action. Is that accurate?

Yeah, that sounds pretty spot on. It's like as soon as I think about starting something new, my mind just goes straight to all the worst-case scenarios. I picture myself losing everything again, and then I think, "Why even bother?" So I just don't do anything and stay stuck.
Okay. So those thoughts that you have are leading you to certain actions and behaviors. What kind of thoughts are you having?

Mostly stuff like "I'm just not cut out for this" and "I'll never be successful no matter how hard I try." I also keep thinking that since my last business failed, there's no reason this one would be any different. It feels like I'm just fooling myself if I think I can actually make it work this time.
Those are some strong beliefs. I wonder though, have you had any success doing other things in the past that you thought were risky? Have you ever done something that was outside your comfort zone?

Well, I did finish my marketing degree while working part-time, which was pretty tough. And I got my current job even though I was really nervous during the interviews. So I guess I've pushed through some scary things before. But this feels different—this was my own business, my own money. That failure just hit way harder than anything else.

Okay, so you've had some experience pushing through difficult situations before, but this particular setback felt particularly impactful. Can you describe a little more about what happened after your first business closed down?

After it closed, I just felt completely drained. I'd put so much into it—late nights, all my savings, tons of research. And when it didn't work out, I told myself I must have missed something obvious, that I wasn't smart enough or disciplined enough. I stopped talking about business stuff with my friends, and I just focused on my regular job to avoid thinking about it. It felt like if I couldn't make that one work, why would any other idea be different?

So after that failure, you started feeling like you weren't good enough, like you made mistakes that led to the loss. And from there, you went into avoidance mode, where you shut down all the opportunities to think about restarting the business. Was that helpful to you?

Honestly, no. It just made me feel worse over time. Avoiding it gave me some temporary relief, but now I'm stuck in this loop where I want to try again but I'm terrified. I feel like I'm just wasting my potential, and that thought is almost as bad as the fear of failing itself.

And yet, you've mentioned that you've overcome some pretty significant challenges before. Like finishing your degree and getting your job despite being nervous. Doesn't that suggest that maybe this time around, you could do it too? Maybe the outcome won't be exactly the same, but you could push through it anyway.

I guess so, but I can't help thinking that my degree and my job were different because there was a clear path to follow. With my own business, there's no guarantee. It's all on me. I mean, you're right that I've pushed through before, but I can't shake the feeling that this time I'm just setting myself up for another failure.

It sounds like you're putting a lot of pressure on yourself to succeed this time, but you're not sure you believe it's possible. I know you're interested in trying again, so let's think about what you'd need to happen for you to decide that this was worth pursuing. What would that look like?

I think I'd need to feel like I could handle it if it didn't work out. Like, if I could tell myself, "Okay, it didn't go perfectly, but I learned something, and I can move on," then maybe I'd be less scared. Right now, I'm just picturing it as this huge disaster that would prove everything bad about me. If I could just see it as a step instead of a final judgment, maybe I'd actually start.

So you feel like you're ready to take steps, but you're struggling with the belief that this is your final chance to succeed. If you look back at the evidence, it seems like you've done things before that turned out well despite initial setbacks. Would you say that that's true?

I was at this friend's potluck and just grabbed something without thinking, and halfway through I realized it had chicken in it. I feel like I failed at something that's really important to me, and now I can't stop thinking about how careless I was.
So you think you let yourself down by eating that meat, but also that you didn't think enough about what you were going to eat beforehand.

Yes, that's it. I just feel like I should have been more careful, you know? I'm a nurse—I'm supposed to be good at paying attention to details. And now I keep thinking, if I could mess up something this basic, what else am I going to mess up? It's like one mistake proves I'm not as committed as I thought I was.
So you're wondering whether your commitment to being vegan is shaky after that meal.

I guess so. I mean, I've never slipped up before, not even once. And now that I have, it's like... maybe I'm not as strong or as ethical as I thought I was. It feels like one mistake undoes everything good I've done for three years.
Okay, so if you weren't vegan and someone asked you if you were vegan, would you say yes?

No, of course not. If I wasn't vegan, I wouldn't call myself one. That would be dishonest. But I am vegan—I live by those values every single day, except for that one moment. But that moment feels like it cancels everything else out.
So you're having trouble believing that you still truly identify as a vegan.

Right. Because if I was truly a vegan, wouldn't I have checked what was in that dish before taking a bite? Wouldn't I have been more careful? I don't feel like I deserve to call myself that anymore, even though I know deep down it was just a mistake. It's like my brain won't let me off the hook.
Well, it sounds like you believe that calling yourself a vegan means you have to always make perfect choices when it comes to food.

Yeah... I mean, doesn't it? If you're vegan, you don't eat meat. Period. There's no room for "oops, I forgot" or "I didn't notice." It just feels like I broke the most basic rule, and now I've lost my right to that label. But when you say it like that, it does sound a little harsh...
It's easy to say that, but it doesn't take into account the fact that we all make mistakes sometimes.

I know you're right. I'd never judge one of my patients this harshly for making a small error. But when it's me, it just feels different. Like I should be held to a higher standard because this is something I care about so much. It's hard to give myself the same grace I'd give anyone else.
So you're saying that the mistakes other people make are less significant than yours because you think they care less about what they do.

I... I never thought of it like that. That sounds almost arrogant when I say it out loud. I guess I do hold myself to a different standard, but I don't know why. Maybe I'm just scared that if I let this one slip go, I'll start making excuses for bigger things down the line.

Yeah, that kind of makes sense. You might fear that if you allow yourself to be a bit loose with this, it will lead to other problems later. So you want to stay strict with yourself, but that strictness isn't helping you. What do you think?

I think you're right. The strictness isn't helping—it's just making me feel miserable and anxious. I can see now that beating myself up over this doesn't change what happened, and it doesn't make me a better vegan. It just makes me a more stressed-out person. But I don't really know how to stop that voice in my head that says I should have done better.

So I wonder if, instead of beating yourself up about the past, you could try focusing on what you need to do moving forward. For example, next time you go somewhere like that, checking what you're going to eat beforehand could help prevent that from happening again.

That's actually a really good idea. I could just ask beforehand or bring my own dish so I know exactly what's in it. That way I'm not relying on memory or guessing. It feels more proactive than just sitting here feeling guilty. Maybe I need to focus on what I can do now instead of what I should have done then.
Exactly. So we talked about bringing your own dish. That's something you could try doing next week, and then we'll look at any changes you made. Does that work for you?

Yeah, that sounds good. I think I can do that. And maybe I'll also try to be a little kinder to myself when I make mistakes. It's going to be hard, but I can at least try to catch myself when I start spiraling into that guilt again. Thanks for helping me see this differently.

You're welcome. Yeah, catching yourself when you start spiraling is important, too. It's part of being honest with yourself and recognizing patterns that aren't helpful. Okay, so we'll meet up again next week to talk about how that went. See you then. Have a great rest of your day.
Hi there, thanks for coming in again today. How are you feeling? And what did we talk about last time?

Hi, thanks. I'm doing okay, I guess. Last time we talked about how I've been feeling kind of... unimportant, I suppose. Like my job as a middle school art teacher just doesn't measure up to what other people do.

Yeah, so it sounds like the job isn't working out well for you right now, but I also hear you saying that you're still really committed to teaching kids art. So you can imagine that would be a pretty tough situation to be in if something wasn't going so smoothly. What were some things that happened recently that made you feel like this?

Well, just last week I went to a dinner party with some old college friends. One of them is a lawyer, another is a doctor, and they were talking about their cases and patients. I just sat there quietly, because what am I supposed to say? "Oh, I taught twelve-year-olds how to mix primary colors today"? It sounds so small compared to what they do.

So the thing that stood out to me was that you felt like what you had to say wouldn't make sense or would sound trivial compared to the topics being discussed. You just wanted to contribute something relevant. That's a pretty frustrating feeling to experience. Can you remember when this started happening more often?

I think it really kicked in about five years ago, when I hit my early forties. I looked around and realized my college friends were all moving up in their careers—getting promotions, buying houses, making a real name for themselves. And I was still in the same classroom, teaching the same lessons year after year. That's when I started feeling like I'd somehow fallen behind.

Okay. So then the idea came along that you haven't really achieved much yet. It's not really worth continuing to work here. Maybe you should look into other options, maybe even leave the profession altogether. When you look at your life right now, what are some achievements you're proud of?

I mean... I've had students tell me years later that my class was the only one they actually looked forward to. And I've helped some really shy kids come out of their shells through art. But when I say that out loud, it just sounds so small. It's not like I'm saving lives or arguing cases in court.

So let me ask you this. On a scale from one to ten, where one is the lowest and ten is the highest, how likely is it that someone else looks down on you and thinks, \"That guy's not worth any respect\"?

Oh, probably a five or six. Maybe higher on a bad day. I know logically that most people don't think about me at all—they're too busy with their own lives. But sometimes I catch myself assuming they're judging me, especially when I'm around successful people.
Okay, so you can understand why you might think that. But have you ever noticed that people usually keep talking about each other regardless of whether anyone else is listening?

I guess that's true. I mean, at that dinner party, nobody actually said anything mean to me or made me feel unwelcome. They were all friendly and asked about my work. It's just that in my head, I was comparing myself and feeling like I came up short. The judgment was coming from me, not from them.

Exactly, so you're taking in information and interpreting it in a way that doesn't quite match reality. Now, I want you to take those words of encouragement from your students and try putting them together with what you heard from your friends. If someone was writing that letter to you today based on everything you've told me, what would they say?

They'd probably say something like, "You helped me find a way to express myself when I couldn't find the words," or "Your class was a safe place for me." I've actually gotten letters like that from former students. I keep them in a box under my desk. But I guess I don't let myself believe them as much as I should.

So you do believe them, but you're just holding them lightly. You don't really give them the weight they deserve. And what I'd like to do now is help you start believing them more strongly. Let me read you a few things from those letters and see if you can find ways to incorporate them into your daily thinking. Here's one from a student who graduated high school. She wrote, "When I walked into your class, I didn't know what to expect. You made me feel comfortable enough to share my drawings. In fact, you encouraged me to paint my feelings instead of copying pictures I saw online. Thanks for helping me discover who I really am." Okay, so she's telling you that you helped her figure herself out. Would you agree with that assessment?

Yeah, I remember her. She was so quiet at first, barely would look up from her desk. By the end of the year, she was showing her work at the school art fair. I guess... I did play a part in that. It's just hard for me to see it as something big, you know?

It's not easy to put ourselves in that position sometimes. Yeah, it's certainly not always easy to recognize the good stuff in our own work. But I think you'll find that if you bring some of these letters into your life, you'll start seeing them in different ways. There's a lot of value in the work that you do. Would you be open to reading a couple more letters?

Sure, I'd like that. I keep them in that box but I almost never open it. Maybe it's time I actually looked at them again and really let the words sink in. I think I've been avoiding them because they make me feel something I'm not used to feeling.

I bet you have. You're experiencing a whole bunch of positive emotions that you're not used to feeling, and you're probably afraid of being overwhelmed by them. Are you willing to go ahead and pick up the box and see what's inside?
I can do that. I'll bring it to our next session, if that's okay. Maybe we can go through a few together. I think having someone else here to help me see them... might make a difference.
Okay, that sounds great. I'm looking forward to hearing what you think about those letters and what happens when you read them. How does that sound?
It sounds a little scary, but also kind of hopeful. I'm willing to try. Thank you for pushing me on this—I think I've been hiding from those letters for too long.

Glad to hear you're open to trying something new. I'm confident you can pull this off. We'll get to the next step in the therapy process once you've had a chance to read those letters. Is there anything else you want to discuss today?
No, I think that's enough for today. I've got a lot to think about. Thanks for helping me see things from a different angle.
Of course. Please reach out to me if you need anything. Until next time!
How have you been?

I've been alright, I guess. Been busy with work and trying to keep up with things, but that reading thing has been stuck in my head. It's hard to shake the feeling that I just failed at something simple.
Yeah, so if you could take me somewhere in time, where'd you wanna be? What's a good place to go from here?

I think I'd go back to before I even picked up that last book. I was actually enjoying reading then, looking forward to it. Now every time I see a book I just think about how I couldn't finish the last one, and it feels like I'm not even a real reader anymore.
So the thought is that because you didn't finish that book, that means you're not a real reader anymore? That's an interesting idea. Why do you think that's true?

Well, it just seems obvious, doesn't it? A real reader finishes books. That's what readers do. If I can't even stick with one book to the end, then what am I? It's like calling yourself a runner but never finishing a race.
That's kind of a good analogy, isn't it? But let's look at some evidence. How many runners do you know who haven't finished a full marathon yet?

I guess plenty, actually. Some of my friends run but they take breaks, do shorter distances, or just jog for fun. They still call themselves runners. But it feels different with reading, you know? Like finishing a book is the bare minimum.

Okay, so there might be other people running around who don't finish marathons but still consider themselves runners. Is there any chance we could find some people who read books but don't always finish them but still call themselves readers?

I suppose... I mean, I've heard friends talk about putting a book down halfway through because they got bored. They didn't seem ashamed of it. But I guess I just hold myself to a different standard. When I do it, it feels like proof that I'm just not good enough at reading.
So the reason you really feel bad when you put a book down is that you feel like it proves that you aren't a good reader?

Yeah, exactly. It feels like evidence against me. Like if I was a capable reader, I would have pushed through and finished it no matter what. The fact that I didn't just confirms something about my abilities - that I'm weak or lazy or not smart enough to stick with something.
It sounds like you have a few ideas about why you stopped. You mentioned feeling lazy, not being smart enough, and maybe lacking capability. Can you list those out?

Sure. I think I'm lazy because I gave up when it got a bit challenging. I'm not smart enough because a smarter person would have understood the book better and wanted to keep going. And I'm not capable because I couldn't do something as basic as finishing a book. It's like all those things are true about me now.
But I wonder if that's really what happened. Let's look at each one separately. So, you give up when it gets challenging. Does that mean you're lazy?

Well... I don't know. I mean, I don't think I'm lazy at work. I put in long hours and handle tough projects. And I keep up with my responsibilities at home. But with reading, I guess I just assume the worst about myself. Maybe it's easier to blame laziness than to think there might be another reason.
And when it comes to intelligence and capability, are there other areas where you've had success recently? Anytime you were challenged by something difficult, did you manage to persist and succeed?

I mean, yeah, actually. Just last month I solved a pretty tricky issue at work that my coworkers were stuck on. My boss even complimented me on it. And I helped my nephew with his algebra homework, which I haven't touched in decades. I guess if I was really not smart or capable, I wouldn't be able to do those things.

Okay, so you're a hard worker and you're intelligent. But the thing that makes you doubt yourself is something that didn't quite work out. And the result is you think that proves you're not a good reader.

Yeah, that's the thing. I focus on that one failure and ignore everything else. It's like that one book is all that matters, and the rest of my life doesn't count. But when you say it out loud like that, it does sound a bit extreme. Maybe I'm being too hard on myself.
I think that's right. So what if you decided to forgive yourself for not finishing that book?

I don't know if I can just flip a switch and forgive myself like that. But I could start by noticing when I'm being too harsh. Maybe I can remind myself that not finishing one book doesn't mean I'm a bad reader. And maybe I could even try reading something lighter, something I actually want to read, without putting so much pressure on myself.

So that's a couple of ideas you've come up with. One, I'll notice when I'm being too harsh on myself. Two, I'll try reading something lighter, something more enjoyable, without having to force myself. Are there any others?

I think I could also talk to my friends about it. They've noticed I've been avoiding books, and they've been asking. Maybe if I let them know what's going on, they could help me get back into reading without feeling like I have to prove something. And maybe I could set a small goal, like just reading a chapter a day, instead of expecting to finish an entire book right away.

Alright, so you're gonna make sure you're not being too hard on yourself, especially if you catch yourself doing that. Then you'll pick up something light, something you enjoy, and you'll tell your friends. And finally, you'll aim to read a chapter a day.

Yeah, I think that sounds like a solid plan. It feels a lot more manageable than what I was trying before. And honestly, just talking about it with you has helped me see that I was blowing things way out of proportion. I feel a little lighter already.
I'm glad we've made some progress today. I'm excited to hear about how you get on with implementing your plan. Thanks for coming in, and I'll see you next week.
Hi there. I'm really glad to be meeting you today. How are you?
I'm alright, I guess. A bit nervous, if I'm being honest. I've never done anything like this before, so I'm not really sure what to expect.

Well, first off, take a deep breath and relax into my chair a little more. You're doing fine. It doesn't matter whether we know exactly what we'll do today or how long our session will last. We can figure that out together. So, tell me about what's been going on. What's brought you here today?

Thanks. Well, uh... I dropped out of college about a month ago. I was really struggling with the coursework and just felt like I couldn't keep up anymore. But now that I've done it, I can't stop thinking about how I should have just pushed through and finished. I feel like I let everyone down.
So when you say you'd like to push through, where does that lead you emotionally?

It just makes me feel... kind of worthless, honestly. Like I had one shot to make something of myself and I blew it. I think about my parents and how they wanted me to finish, and I just feel this heavy weight in my chest. I keep replaying that moment when I decided to leave, wondering if I could have done something different.
That sounds incredibly frustrating, and those feelings of guilt and shame are completely understandable given the situation. Tell me a little more about what happened.

Well, I was majoring in business, and it just got to be too much. I'd always struggled with some classes, but last semester everything piled up at once. I was barely sleeping, couldn't focus, and felt like I was falling further and further behind. I thought dropping out would be a relief, but instead I just feel worse than before.
That sounds tough. And yet, you still feel like dropping out was the wrong decision.

Yeah, I do. I mean, my parents kept telling me to stick with it, that it would be worth it in the end. And now I'm living back at home with them, no job, no degree, nothing to show for it. Every morning I wake up and just think about how I should be in class right now, working toward something meaningful. Instead I'm just... stuck.
Okay, so maybe there were some things that worked in favor of finishing school, but also some things that didn't work out. Are there any other options besides continuing in school?

I guess I could try to find a job, but without a degree, I feel like I'm limited to stuff I don't really want to do. My parents keep hinting that I could go back next semester, but the thought of jumping back into that pressure... it scares me, to be honest. I don't know what the right path is anymore.
Let's start by looking at what you're saying about getting a job. Why did you decide you'd need a job after dropping out?

Well, I can't just sit around my parents' house doing nothing forever. I'm 46 years old, I should be supporting myself. My parents have been good to let me stay, but I can feel the tension there. They don't say it outright, but I know they're disappointed. So I feel like I need to get out there and prove I can at least hold down a job, even if I didn't finish school.
So, getting a job might help alleviate some of the financial pressure, but it might not solve the problem of feeling like you failed.

Yeah, you're probably right about that. Even if I got a job tomorrow, I'd still be sitting here thinking about that unfinished degree. It's like this voice in my head that keeps telling me I made the biggest mistake of my life, and I can't seem to shut it up.
Maybe that voice isn't entirely accurate. Let's look at the evidence. In what ways is it true that you made a big mistake?

Well, I don't have a degree now, so I'm less competitive in the job market. And my parents spent money on tuition that's basically gone to waste. Plus, I'm back living with them at my age, which isn't exactly where I thought I'd be at 46. So those are pretty concrete ways it was a mistake, aren't they?
Absolutely. Now, are there any downsides to dropping out?

I mean... I guess the downside was that I was miserable in school. I wasn't sleeping, I was anxious all the time, and I felt like I was drowning. Dropping out did stop that immediate stress, at least. But then it just got replaced with this guilt and regret, so it's not like I'm better off now either.
So, dropping out stopped the stress, but now you have another form of stress. Is that fair to say?

Yeah, that's fair. It's like I traded one kind of pain for another. At least in school I felt like I was working toward something, even if it was hard. Now I just feel directionless and down on myself. I guess I can't win either way.
What else could you do to change the outcome?

I don't know... maybe I could talk to the school about taking a leave of absence instead of a permanent drop? Or look into a different program that might be a better fit? My parents keep pushing me to go back to the same thing, but maybe there are other options I haven't considered.
There are definitely other choices. Maybe it's time to consider what you actually want from life, rather than just focusing on what you feel you missed out on.

That's a good point. I've been so stuck on what I lost that I haven't really thought about what I could gain. Maybe I need to step back and figure out what I actually want, not just what my parents wanted for me. It's just hard to see past all this regret sometimes.
It's important to remember that you can't control the past, but you can choose how you respond to it. You can choose to dwell on regrets or you can use them to fuel a positive change.

You're right. I've been beating myself up for a month straight, and it hasn't changed anything. Maybe it's time to start thinking about what I can do now instead of what I should have done then. I'm just not sure where to start.
Well, why don't we take it one step at a time? Let's pick three or four things you'd like to accomplish this week. Then we'll see where you stand next week.

Okay, I can try that. Maybe I could start by looking into what it would take to re-enroll in a different program. And I could also... I don't know, update my resume, even if I'm not sure what kind of job I want yet. Small steps, right?
Small steps are great. What else could you add to your list?

Maybe I could try talking to my parents about how I'm feeling, instead of just avoiding the topic. And... I guess I could give myself permission to take a walk or something, just to get out of the house and clear my head. I've been pretty cooped up lately.
Good. That sounds like a solid plan. I'm really glad to hear you're ready to tackle this.

Thanks. I'm still nervous about all of this, but talking to you has helped me see things a little differently. I think I've been so focused on the past that I forgot I still have choices ahead of me. I'll give these small steps a try.
That's great to hear. Just keep in mind that these goals don't have to be huge or perfect. Sometimes the smallest actions can be the ones that lead to bigger changes.
I'll keep that in mind. I guess I've been expecting myself to have everything figured out overnight, and that's just not realistic. One step at a time, like you said. Thanks for listening today.
You're very welcome. I hope you find success with the steps you're taking. I look forward to hearing about your progress next week.
Hi there! Thanks for coming into the room. How are you feeling?
Hi. I'm okay, I guess. A little nervous if I'm being honest. I've never done anything like this before.

So this will be your first time having this kind of session. It makes sense that you'd feel a little bit nervous about trying something different. Have you had any good experiences in the past where you tried something new and found that it worked well for you?

I mean, taking over as manager at the restaurant was new, and that turned out okay at first. But now it just feels like I'm drowning in responsibilities. I don't know if that counts as a good experience anymore.

Well, I think it can be hard to look back on our successes when we're dealing with some challenges right now. Let me ask you a few things about what's going on here. What do you find yourself doing that seems really helpful to cope with the pressure at work?

To be honest, I don't think I'm coping well. I just keep working harder, trying to get through the pile of tasks. Sometimes I skip lunch or stay late, but it never feels like enough. I tried delegating some stuff to my brothers, but then I just worry that they're not doing it right.

Okay, so maybe you haven't been able to relax at work yet because you're worried that everything might go wrong. And you've tried pushing through more hours and delegating, but those aren't quite helping. So what would you say is the biggest challenge for you right now?

The biggest challenge? It's that I can't stop thinking about work even when I'm not there. I'll be at home trying to watch a movie or something, and my mind just keeps running through the inventory list or worrying about the weekend rush. It feels like there's no off switch in my head.
Yeah, so you're thinking about work even though you're not at work. That sounds frustrating. Is it stressful to have those worries pop up in other parts of your day?

Yeah, it's really frustrating. It makes me feel like I'm never getting a real break, you know? Even when I try to relax, my brain won't let me. And then I start thinking that it's never going to change, that I'm just going to be stuck like this forever, always worrying about the restaurant.
Right. So you're thinking that you're never going to be able to relax because you're always thinking about work. Does that sound like something that could help you to feel better?
I... I guess not. When I put it like that, it sounds pretty hopeless. I just don't know how to stop it. It's like my brain automatically goes there, and I can't control it.
Okay, so it sounds like you'd like to come up with a way of stopping those intrusive thoughts from popping up. Are there certain moments during the day when you're less likely to have these worries?

Hmm. Maybe early in the morning, before the restaurant opens. It's quiet then, and there's no rush yet. But as soon as the first customer walks in, it's like a switch flips and I'm back in that worried state.
So it sounds like once the customers walk in, that switches you back into work mode. So what happens after you leave work?

That's the thing — even after I lock up and drive home, I'm still in that mode. I'll be checking my phone for messages from the staff, thinking about the next day's prep. My mind just keeps racing. My brothers tell me to relax, but I feel guilty if I'm not thinking about work.
Right. So you've got some friends who want you to relax, but you feel bad if you're not thinking about work. Is it possible that maybe they're giving advice that doesn't actually make sense to you?

I don't know... I mean, they see me stressed and they want to help. But they don't understand that if I stop worrying, something might fall through the cracks. The restaurant is our family's business. If I mess up, it's not just my job — it's theirs too.

It sounds like your brothers are concerned about you, but they might not realize how much responsibility you take on when it comes to the restaurant. So if you were to talk to them again, what would you want them to hear or understand differently?

I'd want them to understand that I'm not trying to be a workaholic or anything. I just feel like if I let my guard down for one second, everything could fall apart. But I've never really said that out loud to them. I guess I don't want them to think I can't handle the job.

So you're worried that if you talk to them, they'll think you can't handle the job. Yeah, so it sounds like you believe that if you relax, something could go wrong. Can you think of any instances in the past where you took some time away from work and nothing went wrong?

Well... I took a Sunday off last month to go to my cousin's wedding. I was so anxious about it, but I went anyway. When I came back Monday morning, everything was fine. The dishes were washed, the orders were prepped, no disasters. But in my head, I keep telling myself that was just luck, you know? That next time it might not work out.

So you went on vacation, you didn't worry, and you came back and everything was fine. You thought that was luck, but it wasn't luck — it means you handled it successfully. Okay. So let's think about what you need to do tomorrow. First, you should go to bed early tonight. Then tomorrow morning, before opening the doors to the restaurant, you can write down a few important tasks for the day. Then you can go outside and walk around town or listen to music while you eat breakfast. That way you can clear your head and be ready for work when you get there. Sounds good to you?

I mean... it sounds nice, but I don't know if I can actually do that. I'd probably just end up checking my phone the whole time. But I guess I could try it for one morning and see what happens. It's not like I have anything to lose at this point.

Well, I can see why you might be skeptical about it. But if you give it a try, you'll be able to find out whether it works or not. So it's worth a shot. Tomorrow morning, before opening the doors to the restaurant, you can write down a few important tasks for the day. Then you can go outside and walk around town or listen to music while you eat breakfast. That way you can clear your head and be ready for work when you get there. Sounds good to you?
Yeah, okay. I'll give it a shot. Write down the tasks first, then take a real break before opening. It's just one morning — I can handle that. Thanks for the suggestion.
Great. Well, thanks for coming in today. We'll touch base in a couple weeks to see how that morning went and sort out some other strategies for when you get back from work.
Alright, sounds good. Thanks for listening. I'll see you in a couple weeks, and hopefully I'll have something good to report.
Yeah, sure, definitely. See ya then.
How was your weekend?

It was alright, I guess. I went golfing with some friends on Saturday, which was nice. But I found myself thinking about the donation drive I helped organize last week, and it kind of put a damper on things.
So you're going out having fun with friends but you still got caught up in the donation drive stuff. Why do you think that happened?

I don't know... I guess it's just hard to switch off. I was thinking about how many people we helped, but then I started thinking about all the people we couldn't help. It feels like no matter what I do, it's just a drop in the ocean.
Yeah, so there were those thoughts you had about how much it could contribute to helping others but also knowing that maybe it won't be enough. What was the feeling behind those thoughts?

It's this heavy feeling in my chest, like I'm letting people down even when I'm trying to do good. I get this sense that I'm just fooling myself by thinking any of this actually matters in the big picture. It's like I'm running in place and not getting anywhere.

Okay, so part of it is the thought that it doesn't make a difference, that the effort isn't worth it because it's too small compared to the overall problem. And another part of it is this feeling of being a let-down, that if it doesn't seem like it's making a difference, then somehow you've failed. So you're judging yourself based on whether or not the action makes a difference. How did that feel to you?

I never really thought about it that way... I guess I do hold myself to that standard. It's like if I can't fix the whole problem, then what's the point of even trying? But when you say it out loud, it sounds kind of harsh, doesn't it?
Yeah, it sounds pretty tough, right? Like, if something goes wrong, you assume the worst and give yourself a hard time.
Yeah, exactly. I wouldn't talk to my friends that way, and they wouldn't talk to me like that either. It's like I'm my own worst critic... and I never even noticed I was doing it until now.

That's great awareness. That's something that's probably been going on for quite some time. So you've come into therapy a couple of times and haven't mentioned this before, but now you've picked up on it. So why do you think you didn't notice it before?

Good idea. So maybe you'll go to his place this weekend, bring your brother's tools, and watch him demonstrate?

I usually just go quiet and sort of withdraw. I'll say something like, "Whatever you think is fine," even though I know inside that I'm disappointed. Then I'll end up replaying the conversation in my head later, thinking about all the ways the trip could be ruined.
Yeah, so maybe you're wondering why you end up withdrawing instead of talking about how you really feel. Why don't you tell him exactly how you're feeling when he talks about plans?

I guess I worry that if I say how I really feel, it'll start an argument. He's so excited about this trip — it's his retirement, after all — and I don't want to ruin that for him. But then by staying quiet, I feel like I'm just letting my own disappointment build up, and that doesn't seem fair to either of us.

So part of the problem is that you fear starting an argument, but also you recognize that holding onto your negative feelings isn't healthy for either of you. Can you imagine a scenario where you share your true feelings with him while still keeping the trip moving smoothly?

I think I could try saying something like, "I'm feeling a little anxious about this decision, and I need a moment to think it through." That way I'm not blaming him or shutting down — I'm just being honest about where I'm at. It's hard to imagine him getting angry at that, actually.
That makes sense. So you think expressing your anxiety calmly and directly would help him understand your perspective better, without creating conflict. Would that work for you?

It might. I think the hardest part is just getting myself to actually say it in the moment, instead of retreating into my shell. But I can see how being upfront could prevent all that silent worrying afterward. Maybe I'll try it next time we sit down to talk about the trip.

Okay, so you decide to give sharing your feelings a try the next time you talk about planning. You'll tell him you're feeling anxious and need a moment to think it through. Does that sound reasonable?

Yes, it does. I think I was so caught up in predicting the worst that I forgot I could just... pause and be honest. It might feel awkward at first, but it's got to be better than both of us walking on eggshells. Thanks, that gives me something concrete to work with.
Okay, so you'll be open to giving this a try, and hopefully it will reduce the tension around the trip planning. Before we wrap up, did you have anything else you wanted to add or explore?
Not right now. I think this is a good first step — just being able to say what I'm feeling in the moment, instead of letting my thoughts spiral. I'll see how it goes and let you know next time.
Alright, great. I appreciate you sharing your experience today, and I look forward to hearing from you tomorrow. Take care!

That's exactly it. No matter how many hours I put in, there's always this voice in my head saying it's not enough. I'll lie in bed going over spreadsheets in my mind or replaying meetings, wondering what I might have missed. It's exhausting, but stopping feels even worse somehow.
It sounds like there's some fear of failure mixed in here. Maybe you also believe you need to prove yourself by being thorough.

You might be right. I've always prided myself on being reliable and thorough. It's like if I let my guard down for even a minute, everyone will see I'm not as competent as they think. I guess I feel like I have to earn my place every single day.

Yeah, that makes sense. You know you should treat yourself better, but maybe deep down you're thinking if you mess up once, people won't respect you anymore.

Your brain doesn't want to let go yet. It wants you to keep going. And we could try to change that thought process together. Would that interest you?

Yes, I think I need that. I'm tired of running on empty and feeling like I'm constantly failing my own impossible standards. If you can help me find a way to quiet that voice a bit, I'd really appreciate it.

So you've got a couple of options here. One, we could try to gather more evidence about whether other mistakes really mean the end of the world. Or, we could focus on trying to understand why you're having such a strong reaction to the possibility of making a mistake in the first place. Which one would you prefer?

I think understanding why I react so strongly would be more helpful. I've tried the logical approach before - telling myself it's not that bad - but it never sticks. Maybe if I figure out where this pressure comes from, I can finally start to ease up on myself.
Alright, so let's explore where this intense pressure to perform comes from. Let's start by looking back to when you first started this job. What happened during those early days?

When I first started, I was really eager to prove myself. My boss at the time was very demanding - he'd point out the tiniest errors in my reports and made me feel like anything less than perfection was unacceptable. I think I've been trying to avoid that feeling of being judged ever since.
So now you have that memory of the past. That feeling of being judged and scrutinized. Is there another memory that came up as well?

Well, my dad was a lot like that boss, actually. He was a perfectionist too - always pointing out what I could have done better, never really satisfied. I remember bringing home a report card with all As and one B+, and he just focused on the B+. I guess I've been trying to earn his approval my whole life, even though he passed away years ago.
So I hear a connection between your dad and your current boss. They both felt critical, and you reacted by becoming very hard on yourself. It seems like you're carrying around a burden from the past.

Yeah, I never really thought of it that way. I guess I've been trying to meet standards that aren't even mine anymore. My dad's been gone for ten years, and that boss left the company ages ago. But I'm still acting like they're both looking over my shoulder, waiting for me to slip up.
So the past experiences are influencing your present reactions. Does that sound about right?

It does. It's like I'm still that kid trying to get a pat on the head that never comes. I don't know why I can't just let that go. I'm a grown man with a good job and a family - I shouldn't still be chasing approval from people who aren't even here anymore.
Let's take a moment and talk about what it would look like if you weren't so concerned about meeting these external expectations. Imagine you've decided you don't need to impress anyone.

That actually sounds... freeing, in a way. I'd probably leave work at a normal time, have dinner with my wife without my phone buzzing, maybe even take up that guitar I've been meaning to learn. But there's this voice saying it's selfish to slack off, that I owe it to everyone to keep pushing.
Does that sound reasonable to you? Like you're putting others' needs above your own?

I suppose it does. I've always thought being a good person meant putting others first, doing more than expected. But honestly, I'm starting to see that it's just making me miserable. Maybe taking care of myself isn't the same as letting people down.

So you realize that this behavior is hurting you, but you're struggling to stop. You recognize that it's not serving you. Now let's look at some ways to address this issue. Are you willing to experiment with slowing down a bit?
I think I'm ready to try. It's scary, but what I'm doing now isn't working anyway. What did you have in mind?

We could start by setting a time limit on certain tasks. Say, spending only forty-five minutes on each report instead of dragging it out till midnight. Then after that time, you force yourself to move on and check with your team if they have any questions later.

That sounds manageable. I think I could try that with one small task first, maybe a status update that isn't too critical. If I can prove to myself that a quick version won't cause disaster, maybe I can build up to the bigger projects.
So let's pick a low-risk task for your first try. What do you think?

I've got a weekly progress report that I usually spend two hours on. It's really just for internal use - nobody senior even reads it. I could try completing it in thirty minutes this Thursday and see what happens. If nobody complains, that might help me see things differently.
Sounds great. Sounds like a solid first step. We'll see how it goes on Thursday, and then we'll come back tomorrow and discuss it.
Hi, how are you doing? What were we talking about last time?

Oh, hi. I'm okay, I guess. We were talking about that belief I have about writing — that it's a waste of time because of how I struggled with it in school. It's been on my mind a lot since our last session.
