I think it really started back in high school. I had this English teacher who would always mark up my essays with red pen, and I'd get D's no matter how hard I tried. After a while, I just figured I wasn't meant to be a writer, so why bother?
So when you look back now, you're wondering if there was some way around this. You know, maybe you could've done something differently?

I never really thought about it that way. I guess I always just accepted that I was bad at writing and that was that. But now I wonder... maybe if I'd asked for help back then, or practiced more, things could've been different. But it's hard to shake that feeling that it's too late now.
Okay, so what would have to change for you to feel like you still have time?

I'm not sure... I guess I'd need to stop thinking that every single thing I write has to be perfect from the start. But that's terrifying, you know? What if I write something and it's just as bad as it was in school? I don't think I could handle that disappointment again.
Okay, so let me hear your thoughts on that. So first, do you remember having any writing assignments where you actually ended up with a passing grade?

Well... yeah, actually. There were a couple of times I got a C or even a B on some creative writing assignments. But those felt like flukes, you know? Like the teacher was just being nice that day or I got lucky with the topic. The bad grades always felt more real.
Okay, so it sounds like there's a bit of conflicting information here. On one hand, you can remember getting some good marks. And on the other, you feel like the D's were the truth.

That's... that's a good point. I never really stopped to think about it that way. I've just been focusing on all the bad grades for so long that the good ones don't even feel like they count. But I guess they do count, don't they?

They certainly count. They show that you're capable of doing well sometimes. Now, let's say you took that advice and decided to give it another shot. You gave it one try, and somehow you managed to write something good, but it wasn't perfect. Would that mean you should throw it away?

No, I guess not. I mean, if it's good, why would I throw it away just because it isn't perfect? That seems silly when I say it out loud. But in my head, it always feels like if it's not perfect, it's not worth anything at all.
It makes sense that you'd want perfection. It's very important to you that your work looks great and meets your standards. But how does someone else view that piece of writing?

Well, I suppose someone else might see it differently. They might not even notice the flaws I'm obsessing over. My friend Sarah always tells me I'm way too hard on myself about stuff like this. But it's hard to believe her when I've got all those memories of red pen sitting in my head.
But I guess she's right, though. You're putting a little too much pressure on yourself by holding this belief that everything has to be perfect, which is making you feel anxious and overwhelmed.

I think you're right. It's exhausting, honestly, trying to hold myself to this impossible standard. I never really saw it as pressure before — I thought I was just being realistic about my abilities. But maybe I've been tougher on myself than anyone else ever was.
Yeah, I think you're beginning to see that. So what would you suggest as a way to tackle this anxiety? How could you challenge these beliefs?

Maybe I could start small... like, just write a few sentences in a journal every day, without worrying if they're any good. Just to prove to myself that writing doesn't have to be this huge, perfect thing. I could show it to Sarah even if I'm scared — she's always supported me.
That sounds like a solid plan. Can you imagine the positive outcome of that? How might it go down?

I think it would feel scary at first, but maybe after a few days, I'd start to see that the world doesn't end when I write something imperfect. Sarah would probably tell me it's good, and even if she's just being nice, it might help me see that my writing isn't as terrible as I think. Maybe I could even start to enjoy it again, like I did when I was a kid before all that school stuff got into my head.
It sounds like that sounds pretty hopeful. I wonder if you'll want to try that out.

Yeah, I think I will. It's just a few sentences, right? Nothing major. I can always throw the notebook away if it gets too overwhelming. But maybe... maybe it's time I gave myself a real chance to see if I can write without all that fear holding me back.
And I think that's exactly what you should do. How many pages are you going to keep for the next week?

I think I'll aim for just one page a day. That feels manageable — not too much pressure, but enough to actually do something. If I can do that for a week, maybe I'll feel brave enough to try writing something a little longer the week after.
Okay, so you're going to aim to write a page every day for the week. Then you can increase the length later. Is there anything else you want to add to this plan?

Maybe I could write about something I actually enjoy, like memories of my mom getting better after her cancer treatment. Yeah, that's about right. Every time I open up that document, I just hear this voice telling me "Who are you to write about animals? You're just a mall cop." It's like the two things don't belong together in the same person.

There's definitely a connection between being able to talk about parrots and feeling silly when doing so. Is it that you think people will laugh, or is there another reason why you feel silly?

But even though you don't have formal qualifications, wouldn't anyone who knows you'd still find that impressive?

That makes sense. So you've got this idea that you need formal credentials, like a degree, for your knowledge of animals to count, but maybe other people don't see it that way.

Huh. I never really stopped to think about that. I've been so focused on what I don't have—the degree, the fancy title—that I forgot I've got fifty years of watching, reading, and learning. So it seems like you've been putting yourself down quite harshly, but if you look at it from someone else's perspective, that may not be quite so accurate. Maybe try approaching it differently. Instead of thinking, "I'm not qualified," what if you thought, "I've learned a lot about birds over the years"?

I suppose I could try that. It feels strange, like I'm bragging or something. But you're right—I have learned a lot. Okay. Let's try that. Next time you're at the mall or anywhere else, notice that voice coming up. When you catch yourself saying "I'm not qualified" or "I'm a fraud," stop and say instead, "Wow, I've actually learned a lot about parrots." Does that make any sense?

Yeah, I think I can do that. It's just a small thing—swapping one thought for another. I'll give it a try next time I'm walking past that pet store. Maybe I can even stop and watch the parrots for a minute, just as a reminder of what I know. Thanks for that.
No problem. Well, I hope you're feeling better after our chat. I'm glad I could help. Take care!
How are you doing? How was your weekend?

I don't know... maybe it's not just the feedback. Yeah, that's exactly it. It's like a loop in my head. I sit down to paint, and all I can hear is that voice saying, "This isn't good enough. Nobody's going to care. You might as well stop." And then I either freeze or I paint something and hate it before I even finish. It's exhausting.
And how does that feeling of not being good enough affect the way you behave around people? Have you told anyone else about what's happening?

I've barely talked to my artist friends lately. Whenever they ask how my work's going, I just say "fine" and change the subject. I feel like if I admitted I'm struggling, they'd think I'm weak or that I can't handle the criticism. I don't want them to see me as a failure.
So the main goal here is to prevent others from knowing you're having trouble?

I guess... yeah, partly. I don't want them to think less of me. But also, I want to feel like I'm actually good at this again. I want to paint without that constant voice in my head telling me I'm wasting my time. I just don't know how to get back to that place.
Well, let's start by looking at that voice in your head that says you're not good enough and that nobody will care. Let's look at that together.

Alright. That voice feels pretty loud most of the time. It's like it knows all my weak spots and points them out before I even get started. I guess I've never really questioned it—just accepted it as the truth.
So you haven't challenged it. Okay, so this voice inside your head tells you that you're not good enough. What other information do you have that challenges that?

I mean... I do have a few pieces I was proud of before all this started. And I've sold some work, and people have said nice things. But that feels like it was a different person, you know? So it sounds like you still remember the positive experiences you had, but right now you're focusing on the negative aspects. Why do you think that is?

I think... maybe I'm scared that if I let myself feel proud, I'll get lazy and stop improving. Like if I stop criticizing myself, I'll just settle for mediocrity. But the thing is, the criticism isn't helping me improve anymore—it's just stopping me from working at all.
Yeah, it doesn't sound like that criticism is helpful anymore. Does that mean it doesn't need to happen?

I guess not. It's just hard to imagine letting go of that voice. It's been my driving force for so long, even if it's turned against me now. But maybe you're right—maybe I need to find a different way to push myself forward.
So it sounds like you've been using self-criticism as motivation, but it's not getting you where you want to be. What motivates you to succeed when you're feeling down?

When I'm feeling okay, I think what really drives me is the joy of creating something new—seeing an idea come to life on the canvas. I used to get excited about experimenting with color or trying a technique I'd never done before. I miss that feeling.
So there's a difference between how you feel when you're doing great versus when you're struggling. When you're having a good time painting, what's going through your mind?

When it's good, I'm just completely absorbed in what I'm doing. I'm not thinking about how it'll look or what anyone else will think. I'm just playing with paint, making mistakes, fixing them, and enjoying the process. It feels almost effortless, like time disappears. I want to get back to that place.

So you want to get back to that flow state where you're just enjoying the process, but right now your self-critical voice is interfering. How about we try a simple exercise to practice separating those two voices—the constructive one and the destructive one?
I'm willing to try. What do you have in mind? I'm a little nervous about it, but I've been stuck for so long that I'll try almost anything at this point.

So we'll take a piece of paper and write down all the things that the voice that keeps nagging you is saying. Then we'll list all the reasons why you shouldn't believe that voice. Just writing them down should give us a bit of clarity.

Okay, I can do that. I guess it might help to actually see it on paper instead of just having it bounce around in my head. I'll try to be honest about what that voice says, even if it feels uncomfortable.

Great. So grab a pen and paper. On one side, let's write "The Critic," and on the other side, we'll write "Evidence Against The Critic." Okay? Go ahead and jot down whatever comes to mind about what that voice says. Don't worry about organization yet, just let it pour onto the page.

Well... people have bought my work before, so that can't be true that nobody likes it. And I've been painting for over ten years, so I must have learned something about technique. Yeah, that's interesting. So the fact that you've had success with selling work and your professor recognizing your talent are some solid pieces of evidence. You've also mentioned before that you've painted successfully in the past. So what else could add weight to that?

I could also mention that I've won a couple of small awards at local shows, and I've been asked to be in group exhibitions more than once. I guess that doesn't happen if you're completely untalented. It's just so easy to forget all that when the critic is loud.

It's definitely easy to overlook those accomplishments when you're feeling down. So now you have all these reasons to doubt that voice, but what about the actual criticisms? Were they accurate? Are there areas where you could improve?

Exactly. So there's growth opportunities, but you're not a failure. We can separate those ideas. So now you have this written-out critique and you have this evidence against it. What do you think? Which one do you think carries more weight?

So, if you were a parent who played music, do you think your kids would care less about you playing music well? Would they really be more concerned about whether you're a good dad or mom?

Well, that's something worth considering. What else could have been going on? What else could have happened during the concert besides her silence?

I suppose... she was sitting in the front row. She looked nervous the whole time. I remember she was gripping her program pretty tight. Maybe she was just anxious for me? Or maybe she was just focused on watching, not on critiquing. I always jump to the worst conclusion, don't I?

Absolutely. That's probably why you're having such trouble. When things go wrong, you tend to assume the worst, which makes everything seem worse than it actually is. You sort of shut off any possibility of alternative explanations.

I guess I do do that. It's like once I latch onto that negative thought, everything else disappears. I don't even consider that she might have been proud but just not good at showing it. She was a nurse, always practical, never one for big emotional displays. Maybe that's just who she is.

So you think you may be jumping to conclusions based on past experiences. Is there any reason to believe that she wouldn't show her pride now? What would she need to overcome in order to give you a compliment?

I think... she'd have to admit that she's proud of me, and maybe that's hard for her. She's always been the one taking care of everyone, not the one needing to express feelings. That makes sense. So it sounds like there are several reasons why she hasn't given you a compliment yet. One, she's not very expressive. Two, she worries about how you'll respond. Three, she thinks you don't appreciate it.

That sounds like a great idea. I mean, it's better than letting those thoughts fester inside you. What kind of conversation do you think you'd have with her about it?

I'd probably start by just telling her how much that performance meant to me. And then... I'd ask her what she thought about it, honestly. It seems like you have a few ideas about what would work best. Which one do you think would be easiest to try first?

I think the easiest thing would be to just call her and ask how she's doing. Not jump straight into the heavy stuff. Just talk like we normally do, and see if the moment feels right to bring up the concert. If it does, I'll say something simple, like "I was nervous that night, what did you think?" That feels manageable.
Okay, so you'd start with some light conversation, and if that goes well, you'd mention the performance. What would you say if she wasn't too receptive?

I'd probably tell myself that's okay. She might need time to think about it, or she might not be in the right headspace. I could just say, "No worries, we can talk about it another time." And I'd try not to let it ruin my whole day. It's hard, but I think I can manage that.

Good job. You're starting to break down the problem into smaller pieces, which will make it easier to tackle. Okay, so the plan is to pick up the phone tomorrow and have a chat with your mom. See where that takes you, and let me know what happens.
Thanks. I think I can do that. It's scary, but it feels better than carrying all this guilt around. I'll give it a try and let you know how it goes next session.
Sounds good. I hope it works out. Thanks for coming in today.
So I'm gonna start off by checking in with you and just asking about how you're feeling. How are things? How's life been treating you recently?
Well, I've been keeping busy. Work has been piling up, so I've been putting in a lot of hours. I guess that's just how it has to be right now, but I can't say I feel great about it.
It sounds like work has piled up quite a bit. Have you had time to catch up on any other areas besides work?

Honestly, not really. My wife has been mentioning that I'm not around enough, and I know she's right. But when I'm not working, I just feel... restless, like I should be doing something productive. Even meals get rushed.
Yeah, so it seems like you feel kind of overwhelmed by everything going on. What do you think might be happening here?

I think I just feel like I'm not doing enough. Like no matter how many hours I put in or how much I provide, it's never quite enough. Maybe if I just work a little harder or get that next big thing, I'll finally feel like I'm worth something.

Okay. So maybe we can look at what you're saying a little more closely. You mentioned a few different ideas here. First of all, you seem pretty sure that you're not doing enough. And then you also mention that maybe if you worked even harder, or got that next big thing, you'd be able to prove that you were actually worth something.

Yeah, that sounds about right. It's like there's this voice in my head telling me I'm falling short, and it's real loud. Even if I accomplish something at work or buy something nice for the house, it quiets down for a little bit, but it always comes back. I guess I just want to feel like I matter, you know?

Alright. So it sounds like sometimes that critical voice gets quiet, and sometimes it gets louder. Can you tell me where it usually comes from? Where does it come from? Who's telling you those things?

I'm not sure. I guess it might be from my dad. He was always a hard worker, made sure we had everything we needed, but he wasn't around much. I remember him saying things like, "You gotta earn your place in this world." Maybe I took that to heart a little too much.

Yeah, that makes sense. I bet you could imagine how your dad might have felt about himself given his situation, but it doesn't mean that you need to adopt those standards as well. Why don't we take a step back and look at some evidence for and against that idea? What would support the idea that you're not doing enough?

Well, I look around and see other guys my age who are doing better. They've got the nicer cars, the bigger houses, they're further along in their careers. I compare myself to them and I feel like I'm lagging behind. Plus, my wife sometimes gets upset when I miss dinner or work late, and that makes me feel like I'm failing as a husband too.

Yeah. Well, yeah, there's certainly a case to be made that you're comparing yourself to people who might be doing things differently. That's probably because you've noticed that those other people aren't having the same issues that you are. What would be some reasons why you wouldn't agree with that statement though?

I guess when I step back and really think about it, I don't actually know those guys' lives. Maybe they're struggling too, just in different ways. And my wife, she gets upset because she misses me, not because I'm not providing enough. She's told me that before, but I guess I don't really let it sink in.
Right. So you're getting good information from her, but you're not letting it sink in. Why is that? Why isn't that information being processed?

I think because her words don't match the feeling I have inside. It's like I have this belief that I'm not good enough unless I'm constantly achieving something. So even when she says I'm doing fine, I feel like she's just being nice, or that she doesn't see the real picture. That voice inside tells me I need to prove myself, and it drowns out what she says.

So what you're describing here is called cognitive distortions. There's actually some scientific research showing that our brains are wired to search for evidence supporting negative beliefs. So if you believe that you're not doing enough, your brain will actively ignore or minimize positive information and latch onto negative information.

Huh. That actually makes a lot of sense. So my brain is basically tricking me into feeling this way? I never thought of it like that. It's weird to think that I might be creating this whole cycle myself without even realizing it.

That's right. We're doing this to ourselves automatically without even knowing it. It's really important to understand that it's not necessarily intentional. Our goal isn't to blame you. The goal is to find a way to break that cycle and create a more balanced perspective.
So what would breaking the cycle look like? I mean, I've been doing this for years now. It's hard to imagine just turning off that voice or changing the way I think about things.
It might be a process, but we can definitely make progress. One thing we could try is identifying a time when that voice is really speaking up. When do you notice it talking the loudest?

Probably when I'm at work and I see a coworker get praised for something, or when I'm scrolling through social media and see people posting about their vacations or new cars. That's when I really start feeling like I'm not measuring up.
Those are good examples. So what happens after you read something like that or hear someone else get praised? What happens then?

I usually start feeling anxious, like I need to do something right away to catch up. I'll throw myself into work even harder, or I'll start looking online for something to buy. It's like an urge I can't shake until I do something to feel better, even if it's just temporary.
So that anxiety feels like it's driving you to act impulsively to fix the problem. Can you give me an example of when you did something to quell that anxiety?

Last week, my wife mentioned that her friend's husband got a promotion. I didn't say anything, but later that night I was online looking at watches. I ended up buying one that was way too expensive. I told myself I deserved it, but honestly, I just felt worse after it arrived. The whole thing felt empty.

Wow, okay. Okay. So you bought something and it didn't help. In fact, it made it worse. Yeah. So that's really interesting because you wanted to buy that watch, but once you had it, it didn't satisfy you.

Exactly. It's like I'm chasing something that doesn't exist. I thought having that watch would make me feel successful or worthy, but it was just a thing. And now I'm stuck with a credit card bill and the same insecure feeling I started with.
So that experience showed you that even though the purchase offered relief temporarily, it wasn't solving the underlying issue.

Right. It's like putting a band-aid on a broken bone. I keep trying to fix the outside, but the inside's still a mess. I guess that's why I'm here. I need to figure out what's really going on underneath all of this.
And you figured out that that isn't the answer. Yeah. So what are some solutions you can think of that might address the root cause instead of the symptoms?

I think maybe I need to start listening to my wife more when she tells me I'm enough. And maybe stop comparing myself to everyone else. But that's easier said than done, you know? How do I actually make myself believe that stuff?

I guess I'd need to see proof. Not just hear it, but really notice the times when I'm doing okay. Maybe keep track of the good things, like when I finish a project or when I spend time with my family without thinking about work. That might help me see that I'm not falling short all the time.
So you suggested keeping track of the good things. So I wonder if you could write those down each day. So like you said, finishing a project or spending time with your family.

Yeah, I could try that. It sounds simple enough, but I think I've been so focused on what I'm lacking that I don't even notice the good stuff. Maybe writing it down would make it harder to ignore. I'm willing to give it a shot.

That sounds like a great plan. So I think we can agree on that. I want to add one more suggestion. Maybe you could add the date and time for each entry to the list, so you can see exactly when you accomplished something and enjoy it.
That's a good idea. I'll start tonight. Just jot down a few things from today, even if they're small. Thanks, that actually feels like something I can do instead of just feeling stuck.
That sounds really good. I'll leave you alone for a minute and give you a call tomorrow morning. I'll check in on how the journal went and ask if you ran into any challenges. See you tomorrow!

Yes, that's it exactly. I feel like I'd be a fraud, you know? Like, who am I to think I could save animals when I can't even guarantee I'd be able to help every single one? It's like my brain just focuses on the ones I'd lose, and ignores all the ones I could help. I can't shake that feeling.

So it seems like you're putting off making any plans because you're struggling to decide which parent to see during the holidays. Is that right?

Yeah, exactly. I feel like whichever one I choose, the other will be hurt. And if I try to split the day, it'll just feel rushed and fake. I wish there was a way to make everyone happy, but I just don't see how.
It's quite difficult to balance things when you're dealing with this level of change. Sometimes, the hardest part is realizing that it's okay not to solve everything perfectly right away.

I guess you're right. I don't have to have it all figured out today. Maybe I can just take it one step at a time, like the coffee with my mum this weekend. I think I've been putting so much pressure on myself to fix everything that I forget I'm allowed to just feel my way through it.

Yeah, so maybe our plan is to see if this little experiment works out, and if you feel like you should revisit the topic of Christmas later on, then we can look into that. Otherwise, I'll leave it for you to explore on your own.

That sounds like a good plan. I think just having that small goal for this weekend takes some of the weight off. Maybe once I actually do it, I'll feel a bit more ready to think about the bigger stuff like Christmas.
Okay, so the plan is to text your mum and ask her if she'd like to grab a cuppa on Saturday morning. Does that sound reasonable?

Yeah, that sounds reasonable. I'll text her tonight. Thanks for helping me see that I don't have to fix everything at once. It actually feels a bit lighter now, just having one small thing to work on.
I'm glad I could help you see that taking one step at a time is a realistic approach. I hope you have a good evening and that your mum is happy to accept your invitation.
Thanks, I appreciate that. I'll let you know how it goes next time we meet. Have a good evening.
Have a good evening. See you next time.
Hi, I'm glad to see you again. How are you doing? And how's life been since we last met?

Hi. I'm doing okay, I guess. Life's been pretty much the same. Spring is starting to come around, and I'm already feeling that familiar tension, you know? It's like I'm bracing myself for all the crowds.
So you're finding some anxiety about spring coming along? Can you tell me more about that? What kind of situation brings up those anxious thoughts?

Well, it's things like the cherry blossom festivals, or even just a busy park on a sunny weekend. I see people gathering, and my mind just goes straight to feeling trapped, like I can't breathe. I start thinking about all the noise and the jostling, and I just want to get away.

Okay. So there are different levels of crowd situations that bring up these uncomfortable thoughts and feelings. Okay. Is there something else besides the crowded events that comes up? Like, say, a busier time of day, or maybe a busy part of town?

Yeah, actually. Even just walking through the main street downtown during lunch hour gets to me. It's not as bad as a festival, but I still find myself tensing up if there are too many people around. I'll cross the street to avoid a big group, or I'll take a longer route just to stay on the quieter side.

I see. So avoiding busy places is becoming something you do when you feel anxious. Yeah, so the avoidance behavior is helping keep the anxiety down in the moment, but what happens later on? Does it make the anxiety worse overall?

Yeah, I think it does. At the time, it feels like a relief to get away, but later I just feel... disappointed in myself. Like, I missed out on something I actually wanted to do, like grab lunch with a friend. And then the next time, I'm even more scared to try, because I've already proven to myself that I can't handle it.
What makes sense there, and what doesn't? There are some facts that you know that might challenge that thought. You know, you did manage to spend time with your friend at lunch yesterday.

That's true... I did manage that. I guess I just focused on the part where I felt anxious and had to walk a different way. I didn't really think about the fact that I still went and had lunch, and it was actually fine. I guess I sort of forget that part.

Okay. So it sounds like your brain is focusing on one thing, which is the anxiety itself, while ignoring the other positive parts of the experience. And I bet the next time you're faced with a similar situation, you'll remember having lunch with your friend and be able to relax a bit. That sounds very promising.
I hope so. It's hard to hold onto that good feeling, but I'll try to remember it next time. Maybe I can even plan another lunch with him, somewhere that's not too crowded, to kind of build on that.
So you could plan to go to lunch sometime soon and make sure you choose a place that's relatively quiet. I wonder if that would help you build confidence a little bit.

Yeah, that sounds like a good idea. There's a café a few blocks away that's usually pretty quiet in the afternoons. I could suggest that. Maybe if I start with something small like that, I can work my way up to busier places.
So that sounds like a great plan to tackle this step by step. It may take a couple of weeks, but I think you'll find that you can gradually work your way up to bigger crowds over time.

I think so too. It's just hard to be patient with myself, you know? I want to be able to just enjoy spring like everyone else, without all this planning and worrying. But I guess taking small steps is better than just giving up on it completely.

It sounds like you have a good plan going here, and I look forward to hearing how it goes. Would you like to take any action items from our session to implement now, or do you need a little more time to consider it?

No, I think I'm good. I'll text my friend about that café later today. Thanks for helping me see that I actually can do some of these things, instead of just thinking about all the ways it could go wrong. I'll let you know how it goes next time.
Yeah, that sounds like a wonderful plan, and I'm looking forward to hearing about how it works out. Have a great weekend, and talk to you next week. Bye!
Hello. I'm glad you're here. How are you feeling? What did you do yesterday?

Hi. Thanks for having me. I'm feeling okay, I guess—a bit frustrated, honestly. Yesterday I mostly stayed in my dorm and tried to study, but I kept getting distracted by the tape on my glasses. It's hard to focus when you're constantly reminded that something's broken.
So you're telling me that the glasses taped up were distracting you from studying.

Yeah, exactly. Every time I look down at my notes, the edge of that bright tiger print tape comes into my peripheral vision. It's like a little neon sign saying "you're stuck with these ugly things forever." I just end up staring at the tape instead of my books.
It sounds like the tape reminds you about how much you want to wear your glasses.

I think it's more than that. It's like... the tape is a constant reminder that I can't just go get new ones. I've been to a couple of stores and tried on frames, but nothing feels right. They all look wrong, feel wrong. It's like if it's not exactly my old pair, there's no point. So I'm just stuck with this broken, taped-up mess.
That makes sense. You really value style and appearance. That seems important to you.

It's not just about looking good, though. Those glasses felt like *me*. I'd had them for years—they were part of my identity. When I look in the mirror now with this tape, I don't recognize myself. And trying on other frames... it's like I'm trying to wear someone else's face. I don't know how to explain it without sounding dramatic.
Okay, so the glasses aren't just an accessory, then. They're a part of who you are.

Yes, exactly. They're like this extension of myself that I've had for so long. When they broke, it felt like losing a piece of my identity. And the thought of replacing them with something different feels like I'm being forced to become someone I don't want to be. It's like there's no middle ground—either I have my old glasses or I have nothing.

Okay. So you need to keep the glasses, but the frame doesn't fit anymore. So maybe it's not possible to get them back in their original condition. But maybe there's another way to fix them that wouldn't involve changing the whole frame. Maybe you could find a shop that specializes in repairing glasses. Or maybe you could try to make a template that will give the glasses the shape you like, but still leave them recognizable as your own.

I hadn't really thought about that. I guess I assumed once they broke, that was it—either get exactly the same pair or give up. But finding someone who could actually repair the frame itself... that might be different. The arm snapped right at the hinge, so it's not just a screw that needs tightening. But maybe a specialist could do something. It's a small idea, but it makes me feel a little less stuck, you know?
That does sound like it could work. Have you considered going somewhere else to get the glasses fixed?

Not really. I've been so caught up in the "all or nothing" thinking that I didn't even consider other options. I think I've passed by a little repair shop near campus a few times—they have a sign about fixing watches and jewelry. Maybe they do glasses too. I could at least go in and ask. It's just... what if they can't fix them either? Then I'm back to square one.
And what if you went to that shop and they told you they couldn't fix them either?

I guess I'd be disappointed. Really disappointed. But maybe it wouldn't be the end of the world. I'd have to admit that those glasses are really gone, and then... I don't know. I'd have to start looking at frames again with a different mindset. Not trying to find an exact copy, but something that could become a new "me" in its own way. It's just hard to picture that right now.

Well, let's explore some of these ideas together. Maybe we'll take a trip to that repair shop tomorrow morning. We'll try to fix your glasses. If they can't, well, then you'll have to look around for a replacement, and that's fine.

Really? You'd come with me? That actually helps a lot. I think just having someone else there would make it less overwhelming. If they can fix them, great. If not, maybe I could actually try on a few pairs without feeling like I'm betraying my old ones. I guess I've been avoiding the whole situation because I was afraid of having to make a decision alone. Thank you.
There's always a chance that they won't be able to help. But maybe we'll find that the repair shop can do it. Or maybe we'll find something better for you. And either way, we'll figure it out.

That's... actually comforting to hear. I've been so focused on the worst-case scenario that I forgot there might be other outcomes. And even if it is the worst case, I guess I'd survive. Maybe I could even find a pair I like—it's just scary to admit that change might not be all bad. Okay. Let's try it tomorrow.
Tomorrow sounds good. See you then.
See you then. I'll try not to think about it too much tonight. Thanks for listening—it helped more than I expected.
No problem. And hey, remember to breathe.
Hi there. I've been really looking forward to speaking to you again. How are things going?
Oh, hey. Thanks for having me back. I'm alright, I guess. Still got that hunting thing on my mind, you know? It's been a couple months now and I just can't shake it.
Yeah, so we talked about that last week. So how are you feeling right now?
Honestly? Still pretty down about it. Every time I pick up my gear or even see a hunting show on TV, I just feel like a failure. I keep thinking I'll never be good enough at it.
So that failure mindset is making you feel quite frustrated and discouraged by this situation.

Yeah, exactly. It's like I had this one bad trip and now I can't see myself ever doing it right again. My buddies are already planning our next trip and I'm just dreading it. What's the point if I'm just gonna mess it up?
Yeah, it sounds like you're putting a lot of pressure on yourself here. And then when things don't go perfectly, you're telling yourself that it's all your fault.

Well, isn't it? I mean, I practice, I know the land, I do everything right, and then I come back empty-handed. Everyone else in our group got something that trip. I was the only one who failed. That's gotta say something about me, right?
What do you think about that? Does that sound fair? Is there any other way to look at it?

I don't know... I mean, I guess it could be bad luck or the wind was wrong or something. But that feels like making excuses. A good hunter should be able to work around that stuff, shouldn't he? I keep thinking real hunters don't come home empty.
Okay, but what about other hunters that aren't part of your group? Would those people also be successful hunters?

Well, I guess not all of them. I've heard plenty of stories about even experienced guys having bad seasons. But that's different - they've already proven themselves. They've got years of success behind them. I'm still trying to prove I belong out there.
And yet, you don't seem very sure you fit in.

No, I guess not. I mean, I've been hunting since I was a kid with my dad. I know the basics. But that one trip... it just made me feel like I'm fooling myself. Like maybe I'm just not cut out for it the way other guys are.
Yeah, well, you might not be cut out for being a trophy hunter. You could probably hunt deer for dinner all year round.

Ha, that's true. I do bring home meat most years. Maybe I'm getting too caught up in the whole "big buck or nothing" thing. It's just hard not to compare myself to the guys who always seem to nail it. But you're right - I've never gone hungry.
Right. And how much does success matter? Does it matter? Is it important?

I mean, yeah, it matters. But maybe not as much as I've been telling myself it does. When I think about it, the best part of hunting is just being out there with my buddies, the quiet mornings, that kind of thing. The kill is just... part of it, I guess. Not the whole thing.
That's great to hear. You've got some really important elements of what makes hunting special.

Thanks. I think I needed to hear that. Maybe I've been so focused on the end result that I forgot why I started hunting in the first place. It's not just about bringing something home - it's about the whole experience.
It certainly doesn't have to be about trophies. Sure, it can be, but it doesn't have to be.

Yeah, you're right. I think I've been putting way too much pressure on myself. Next time I go out, I'm just gonna focus on enjoying the time with my buddies and being in the woods. If something comes my way, great. If not, well... there's always next time.
And I bet if you change that perspective, it will help you enjoy the outdoors more.

I think so too. I'm actually feeling a bit better about that upcoming trip now. Maybe I'll even talk to my buddies about how I've been feeling - they're good guys, they'd probably understand. Thanks for helping me see this differently.

Anytime. I'm glad I could help. Let me give you one more idea before we wrap up. What if you told yourself that maybe you wouldn't succeed in bringing down a big game animal that day? But that it wouldn't necessarily mean you were a failure.

That... actually makes a lot of sense. I think I can try that. Just take it one day at a time and not judge my whole self-worth on one hunt. I appreciate you saying that. I'll give it a shot next time I'm out there.
Absolutely. You may find that once you start focusing on enjoying the moment instead of worrying about results, you'll notice your confidence starts rising.
Hi, good morning. I've been meaning to catch up with you and talk about how things are going with work lately. So do you want to start off by telling me what's happening?

Morning. Yeah, I suppose it's been a rough few months. After every gig with my band, I just can't shake this feeling that I've messed up, even if most of it went well. It's like that one bad moment sticks with me and ruins the whole night.

So that's what we're focusing on today, then. When you feel like you've messed up after a gig, what kind of thoughts go through your head? What's happening inside your mind when that thought comes up?

I just keep replaying that one song — the one where I hit a wrong note or the timing was off. And then I tell myself that I'm not good enough, that the audience probably noticed, and that my bandmate must be disappointed in me. It's like the rest of the set doesn't even count anymore.
Okay, so when you're performing, there's something going on in your mind that makes you think that you're not good enough because of one mistake. Is that right?

Yeah, exactly. It's like I'm up there trying to be perfect, and the second I slip up, I forget all the songs that went right. It's not even about what the audience says or does — they usually clap and seem happy — but in my head, I've already decided it wasn't good enough.
So when you play, you think that everything depends on that one part. Does that make sense?

It does, yeah. Like, if I'm not flawless, then the whole performance was a waste. I know it sounds a bit extreme when I say it out loud, but in the moment, it feels completely true. My bandmate always tells me to relax, that nobody's perfect, but I can't seem to let it go.
Right, so I wonder if your bandmates view performances differently from you. Do you think they put as much pressure on themselves to perform perfectly?

No, not really. My friend, the drummer — he's way more laid back. He laughs off mistakes and says it's part of live music. I wish I could be like that, but I can't help feeling like I've let him down when I mess up. I think he's tired of me bringing it up after every show, honestly.
Okay, so you feel like your friend is annoyed that you're dwelling on this stuff too much. But what if it were someone else who made that one mistake instead of you? Would you be as hard on them?

That's... actually a good question. No, I wouldn't. I'd probably just tell them it's no big deal, that everyone has off moments. I've said that to him before when he's dropped a beat. So why can't I give myself that same break? It just feels different when it's me, you know?

Okay, so it seems that maybe your friends don't treat mistakes quite like you do. You treat them pretty harshly, whereas others are more lenient. Can you tell me any other people who might react similarly to you?

I don't think I know anyone who reacts this way, honestly. Most musicians I've met are pretty easygoing about slip-ups — they just move on. I guess I'm the only one who gets stuck on it. It's like I have this voice in my head that won't let me forgive myself for not being perfect.

Well, I think that's a great place to start. We'll try to come up with some ways to challenge that internal voice later on. So let's look at your overall goal. You mentioned that you want to feel better and less anxious during gigs. Right. How do you think achieving that goal will affect your day-to-day life outside of playing music?

I think it would make a huge difference. Right now, after a gig, I'm in a bad mood for days — I don't feel like practicing, I'm irritable, and I avoid hanging out with my bandmate because I'm embarrassed. If I could let go of that, I'd probably enjoy music again and feel closer to my friend. It's affecting more than just the stage, that's for sure.

So you want to improve your mood, reconnect with your friend, and get back into enjoying music. Those sound like important goals for you. Now let's explore how you currently respond to those situations. When you realize you've made a mistake, what do you typically do immediately afterward?

I usually go quiet and just focus on finishing the set. I don't joke around or smile like I normally would. After the show, I'll replay the mistake over and over in my head, and sometimes I'll apologize to my bandmate, even if he says it's fine. Then I'll go home and just feel down for the rest of the night.
So when you make a mistake, you tend to stay silent and withdraw emotionally. That seems to happen a lot. Do you notice if you behave that way after other kinds of mistakes too?

Huh, I never really thought about it that way. But yeah, I guess I do. If I mess up something small in daily life — like forgetting an appointment or burning dinner — I get pretty down on myself too. I'll beat myself up about it and kind of shut down for a while. It's not just the music, is it?
Not just music, yes. So it's not just about playing guitar. It's more about making mistakes in general, right? You get upset when you make mistakes anywhere, whether it's music or something personal.

Yeah, I think that's spot on. I never connected the dots before, but it's true. I hold myself to this crazy high standard in everything, and when I fall short, I feel like I've failed as a person. It's exhausting, honestly. I just want to be able to mess up and move on like everyone else seems to.

Yeah, I totally understand. There's definitely some self-criticism and negative behavior involved here. Let's take a step back. So you're having a difficult time letting go of mistakes, which is causing you anxiety. This anxiety is leading to withdrawal and a bad mood, and you're wondering if there's another way to handle this. Are you open to exploring that?
Yes, I am. I'm tired of feeling this way, and I don't want to push my friend away or lose my love for music. If there's another way to handle it, I'm willing to try. I just don't know where to start.

Okay, so let's think about this a little more carefully. What's happening when you make a mistake? First, you have a thought that you messed up. Then you start beating yourself up mentally, withdrawing socially, and putting yourself down. Okay, so there's a sequence of events here. The first thing is you make a mistake, and then you develop certain thoughts and behaviors. So if you change those thoughts and behaviors, would that change your outcome?

I suppose it would. If I could stop that spiral before it really takes hold — maybe tell myself it's just one mistake, not the end of the world — I might not get so down. And if I didn't withdraw, I could probably still enjoy the rest of the night with my bandmate. It sounds simple when you put it like that, but in the moment it feels impossible.

Absolutely. So you're saying that if you could find a different response to that initial thought, you'd be happier. And you also believe that finding an alternative action would help. So if you were to try that approach tomorrow, what would you need to prepare beforehand?

I think I'd need to remind myself before the gig that mistakes are allowed. Maybe write down a few simple things I can say to myself when I feel that panic coming — like "it's just one note" or "the audience doesn't care as much as I think." And I'd have to promise myself not to apologize or bring it up afterward unless my bandmate does first. That could be a start.
Sounds like a solid plan to me. So you're basically saying that you can control what you do and what you think, even though you can't control what happens on stage. That's an interesting perspective.

Yeah, I never saw it that way. I've been trying to control the performance itself, making it perfect, but that's impossible. Maybe I should focus on controlling my reaction instead. That feels a bit more manageable, honestly.

Alright, so you're planning to use a phrase that reminds you that mistakes are okay, and you're going to decide not to dwell on the error once it happens. That's a good plan. Before you leave, is there anything else you'd like to add?
No, I think that's plenty to work on for now. I'll give it a try at our next practice session and see how it feels. Thanks for helping me see this from a different angle — I appreciate it.
You're welcome. I hope it works out well for you. Just remember, we can revisit this anytime if you'd like to discuss it further.
Thanks, I'll keep that in mind. I'll let you know how it goes next time we meet. Have a good day.
Me too. Take care, and I'll speak to you soon.
Hi there, how was your weekend?

Oh, it was alright, I suppose. I spent most of it in the garden, but I couldn't really enjoy it. Kept finding myself staring at that one plant I trimmed too much, and then I'd just feel anxious about the whole garden looking ruined now.
So anxiety about that one plant affected your ability to spend time in the garden?

Yes, exactly. I mean, I was out there, but my mind was just stuck on that one spot. I'd look at the other flowers and vegetables, and they look fine—healthy, even—but I can't seem to shake the feeling that it doesn't matter because that one plant is ruined. It's like my whole garden is spoiled now.
Yeah, so if that one plant is gone, the rest of the garden isn't worth saving either. And maybe it is.

Well, when you say it like that, it sounds a bit extreme. But that's honestly how it feels. I know the tomatoes are still growing and the roses are blooming, but my brain just keeps saying, "What's the point? You messed up one part, so the whole thing's a failure." I can't seem to stop thinking that way.

So you've got some thoughts running around in your head, and it makes sense why you're spending more time looking at the damaged area than the healthy parts. So that's a good sign you're noticing that pattern going on. What would happen if we tried to change those thoughts?

I'm not sure I understand what you mean. Change them how? I've tried telling myself the garden's still nice, but it doesn't feel true. It's like there's a voice in my head that just won't let go of that plant. I suppose I could try focusing on the other plants more, but it feels dishonest somehow, like I'm ignoring the problem.
So it feels like acknowledging the problem, which is fair enough, but it also feels like ignoring the other stuff. What do you think might be happening here?

I suppose... maybe I'm only seeing the bad part. Like, when I walk out there, my eyes just go straight to that trimmed plant and everything else fades away. Even the nice parts seem less important. I guess I've never thought about it that way before—that I might be choosing to see only the one thing that went wrong.

Okay. So, you're noticing that something's happening when you walk into the garden and you're choosing to see just the one spot, right? Maybe we could try to make things easier for you by making your eyes take you somewhere else.

That sounds like it might help. I mean, I could try walking to the other side of the garden first, maybe look at the tomatoes or the lavender. I'm just worried that even if I do that, my mind will still wander back to that plant. But I suppose I won't know until I try, right?
Sure. You'll find out if it works and whether your mind wanders, but you don't have to worry about having to keep coming back to the plant afterward. Just trying to notice where your attention is.

That's a good way to put it—just noticing. I'm so used to fighting my thoughts or getting upset with myself for looking at the plant. Maybe I can just say, "There I go again," and then gently look at something else. I'll give that a try this afternoon when I water the garden. Thank you.
It sounds like you've found a good solution for yourself. I'm glad to hear that. How does that sound?

It sounds... hopeful, actually. A bit strange, but hopeful. I think I've been so caught up in being upset about that one mistake that I forgot I could choose to look at the rest. I'll let you know how it goes. I might still feel a bit anxious, but at least I have something new to try.
That sounds great. Well, thanks for chatting.
Thank you for listening. It's nice to talk to someone who doesn't just tell me to stop worrying. I'll see how it goes and maybe we can talk again sometime. Take care.
You're welcome. See you later. Bye-bye.
Hi there. How was your weekend?
It was alright, I guess. Spent most of it around the house, did a little work on the deck out back. Kept me busy, which is good.
I'm glad that you got some things done. Did anything happen that upset you while you were doing that?

No, not really. It was just a regular weekend. But I did drive past a sporting goods store on Saturday, and it got me thinking about hunting season coming up. That kind of put a damper on the rest of my day.
So you're wondering if maybe you should sign up for this season. What do you think might happen if you decide not to go?

Well, if I don't go, I'll miss out on something I used to love. My girls will be disappointed too—they keep asking me to take them out like I used to. But if I do go, I just keep picturing something going real wrong.
Yeah, but can you tell me more about what you imagine could go wrong?

I keep seeing myself making a stupid mistake with the rifle, you know? Like tripping while I'm carrying it, or not paying attention and having it go off. It was just a little graze last time, but what if it's worse next time? I can't stop thinking about that.
Okay, so the idea of not going away because you might make a mistake keeps coming up.

Exactly. And I know I've been hunting for years without any real trouble before that accident. But now it's like my brain won't let me forget how close it was. I just feel like it's bound to happen again, only worse.
Okay, so you want to go and hunt with your daughters, but you're worried that something bad will happen. So that's why you're hesitating.
Yeah, that's it spot on. Part of me knows I'm being ridiculous—I've handled guns safely my whole life. But the other part of me is just stuck on that one bad moment. I hate feeling stuck like this.
We need to sort out what's happening here. I'd like to write down those three parts: the good, the bad, and the ugly. Are we okay with that?
Sure, go ahead. I mean, if writing it down helps make sense of this mess in my head, I'm willing to give it a try. What do you need me to do?

What I'd like you to do is pick a place where you can relax and reflect on all that you've told me. Think about what you believe is the truth—that you've had success before—and then jot that down. Then, look at the other side. You're scared about getting hurt again. Write that down. Finally, come up with a third option—maybe even a fourth. Something in between. Take your time and start writing when you're ready.

Alright, I can do that. So I'd write down something like "I've been hunting safely for over twenty years and nothing bad happened." Then on the other side, "I'm scared I'll have another accident, and it'll be worse this time." For a third option... maybe "I could start with a short trip, just a few hours, and take it slow." That sound about right?
That sounds perfect. When you're done, send it to me by email, and we'll take a look together. Thanks.
Will do. I'll try to get that written up tonight and send it your way. Thanks for listening and helping me sort this out.
Thanks for trusting me with that.
No problem. I appreciate you not just telling me to get over it. Nobody's really done that before.
Right. I appreciate that. Yeah, I'm sure that came across well. See you soon.
See you next time. Thanks again.
Take care. Bye-bye.
Hi there. I'm really glad you're here today. How has life been for you? What's going on in your world lately?

Hi, thanks for having me. Honestly, life's been pretty tough lately. I mean, work is fine, but the whole commute situation... it's really been getting to me. I just feel on edge all the time, especially on the subway.
So you're noticing some physical sensations of anxiety when you're on public transport, and that seems to be affecting how you feel overall. Can you tell me more about those physical symptoms?

Yeah, it's like my heart starts racing and my palms get all sweaty. Sometimes I feel this tightness in my chest, especially when the train is packed and I can see people looking around. I just want to disappear into my seat.
I bet that feeling is really uncomfortable for you. You mentioned wanting to disappear into your seat. Does that happen sometimes when you think something bad might happen on the train?

Yeah, exactly. Like, I start thinking that someone's going to suddenly laugh at me or say something mean. I imagine them looking at me and thinking I look awkward or stupid just standing there. It's like I can almost hear what they're thinking.
It sounds like you've got some very vivid imagery in your head right now. Would you mind telling me a bit more about where you first started hearing other people's thoughts?

Well, it wasn't always this bad. A few months ago, I just noticed this woman staring at me for a really long time. She had this look on her face, like disgust or pity or something. Ever since then, I've been noticing more and more people giving me that same kind of look. Now I can't help but feel like everyone's judging me.
Okay, so you were sitting on the train and you noticed this woman staring at you. After that incident, did you notice any changes in the way you felt afterwards?
